It is common to see claims that the minihalo in Perseus requires some continuous reacceleration or injection (e.g. continuous hadronic production of leptons) to explain its extent, but this is clearly not the case in the models here. As reviewed elegantly in Brunetti & Jones (2014), the argument for reacceleration (or some extended hadronic injection) depends on a number of strict assumptions which are not true in the models we consider here, and removing even one of those strict conditions makes it fairly easy to understand how the minihalo could be produced without reacceleration. From most-to-least important, these prior assumptions are: (1) Models often assumed CR transport is purely diffusive, so the transport time to distance 𝑟scales as Δ𝑡∼ 𝑟2/𝜅∼30 Gyr (𝑅/100 kpc)2 (1029 cm2 s−1/𝜅), as compared to including any streaming component giving Δ𝑡∼𝑟/𝑣st ∼ 1 Gyr (𝑅/100 kpc) (100 km s−1) (Pfrommer & Enßlin 2004; Vazza & Botteon 2024). That quadratic-versus-linear difference means that even a small streaming speed will almost always dominate bulk transport at large radii ≳ 100 kpc, and order-of-magnitude reduces the transport time of CRs (shorter Δ𝑡at large 𝑅by a factor 𝜅/𝑣st 𝑅 ∼ 0.003 (𝜅/1029 cm2 s−1) (100 km s−1/𝑣st) (Mpc/𝑅)). Note that the “streaming” term here can arise from advection/convection, Alfvénic or super-Alfvénic streaming as in self-confinement models, super-diffusion (Liang & Oh 2025), or simply a gradual radial decrease of the CR scattering rate (𝜈cr ∝1/𝑟, so 𝜅∝𝑟) – these all have the same effect, for our purposes. (2) In addition to neglecting streaming, reacceleration models often assume extremely low diffusion coefficients, as low as 𝜅∼1027 cm2 s−1 (or even the fully-trapped limit 𝜅+ 𝑣st 𝑅→0, see Sarazin 1999; Brüggen et al. 2002; Enßlin et al. 2007; ZuHone et al. 2013), which are based on decades old “leaky box” type models for LISM CRs that have been widely shown to be biased and order-of-magnitude incorrect, as compared to modern fits with codes like GALPROP, DRAGON, PICARD, USINE, and others that robustly give 𝜅eff (accounting for the weighted-energy-average and for streaming/advective/convective speeds adopted as well) about two orders of magnitude larger (see e.g. De La Torre Luque et al. 2021; Zhao et al. 2021; Korsmeier & Cuoco 2022; Hopkins et al. 2022b,b; Di Mauro et al. 2024; Jacobs et al. 2023; Tovar- Pardo et al. 2024; Silver & Orlando 2024; Recchia & Gabici 2024; De La Torre Luque & Linden 2024; Ramírez et al. 2024). Assuming a very low 𝜅has a double effect: it increases the diffusion time (assuming diffusion only) as ∼𝑅2/𝜅, but also increases the reacceleration rate as ∼(𝑣𝐴−¯𝑣𝐴)2/27 𝜅, so the ratio of diffusion-to-reacceleration time scales ∝(𝑅𝑣𝐴/𝜅)2. (3) Reacceleration models generally neglect multiple sources, despite the plethora of known radio sources in Perseus and other SCCs. This is important especially for the giant halo and any structure at ≳100 kpc. Per § 3.5.2, beyond 𝑅≳100 kpc, if CRs travel more than ∼100 kpc from their individual galaxy sources, they will “overlap” each other’s minimini-halos. This means that the effective “travel distance” required for any CR is really never more then 𝑅local mini ∼100 kpc, even if the galaxies being considered are globally at 𝑅∼1 Mpc from the cluster center. This reduces the maximum travel time from ∼3000 Gyr (𝑅/Mpc)2 (1029 cm2 s−1/𝜅) for a single source to ∼1 Gyr (𝑅local mini /100 kpc) (100 km s−1/𝑣st, eff). (4) Some of the historical models have assumed unphysically high loss rates for CRs. In particular some (see discussion in Jaffe 1977; Gitti et al. 2002; Brunetti & Jones 2014) invoked

fields as strong as 𝐵≳50 𝜇G at 𝑅≳100 kpc, equivalent to 𝛽≪1 (or simply assumed 𝛽= 1, i.e. equipartition fields; Brunetti et al. 1997; Abe et al. 2024). Today this is clearly ruled out by multiple observational constraints (see § 3.5.3), and is far larger than the predictions of any cosmological models (Dolag & Enßlin 2000; Dolag et al. 2002; Borgani & Kravtsov 2011; Hopkins & Raives 2016; Hopkins 2016; Donnert et al. 2018; Barnes et al. 2018; Ponnada et al. 2025; Nelson et al. 2024; Whittingham et al. 2024). But it would have again the dual effect of making CR loss rates much faster (loss time ∝𝐵−2 in this limit) while making reacceleration rates larger (∝𝑣2 𝐴∝𝐵2). (5) In the reacceleration term in the CR equations-ofmotion (in historical reacceleration models), CR scattering is almost always implicitly assumed to be perfectly isotropic, “grey” (pitch angle-independent), and gyro-resonant, with zero streaming motion (zero anisotropy in the distribution function of CRs, effectively ∇𝑃cr = 0). This gives the traditional expressions for reacceleration (Ptuskin 1988).10. But this is actually the maximum-possible reacceleration term. As discussed in Hopkins et al. (2022b,c); Hopkins (2023) at the energies of interest (∼GeV), if CR self-confinement plays any significant role in exciting scattering, or even if it does not (in pure extrinsic turbulence models for scattering) if the CRs are (on average) propagating down gradients in density and |B| (which they are, by definition, here, to reach larger 𝑅) then these should not be symmetric, which means |¯𝑣𝐴| ∼𝑣𝐴and the reacceleration rate is reduced by a significant factor. Moreover as shown in both analytic derivation and direct numerical simulation in e.g. McKenzie & Webb (1984); Begelman & Zweibel (1994); Bustard & Oh (2022), almost any anisotropy/streaming/∇𝑃cr, or finite-wavespeed effects if 𝛽> 1, will suppress any non-resonant reacceleration by orders of magnitude (so the reacceleration rate scales ∝1/𝜅gyro ∝𝜈gyro cr , not 1/𝜅tot ∝𝜈tot cr ; see also Tsung et al. 2022; Sampson et al. 2025). But in extrinsic turbulence models (the only models where reacceleration occurs) in clusters, the resonant scattering (proportional to 𝐷𝑝𝑝) is suppressed by many orders of magnitude owing to a combination of anisotropy and damping (Chandran 2000; Yan & Lazarian 2002; Yan & Lazarian 2004; Lazarian 2016; Kempski & Quataert 2022; Hopkins et al. 2022c). Consistent with these arguments, LISM CR observations coupled to Galactic CR transport models have found growing evidence against significant reacceleration (e.g. Orlando et al. 2015; Jóhannesson et al. 2016; Gabici et al. 2019; Hopkins et al. 2022b; Silver & Orlando 2024; Di Mauro et al. 2024, and references therein). Taken together, this explains not only why the models here do not “need” reacceleration (or extended hadronic injection) to explain the mini and giant radio halos, but in fact we find reacceleration (even in the limits above where it would be strongest) is at most a weak correction to our predictions. We do stress the reacceleration we refer to here is specifically “diffusive” or “turbulent” reacceleration (the term often parameterized as “𝐷𝑝𝑝” in CR models): reacceleration by large-scale, powerful convective compression (large compressive ∇·u) or first-order Fermi (re)acceleration in shocks (DSA) from e.g. cluster mergers, are still plausible sources of largescale CR acceleration in extreme merging clusters (but obey qualitatively different scalings).

4.3. Why Isn’t Inverse Compton Already Ruled Out in X-Rays? As discussed in § 3.2-3.3, at ∼0.1 −100 keV in X-rays, observations appear to be perfectly consistent with much of the apparent SCC cooling luminosity at ≲100 kpc coming from CR-IC rather than thermal emission. This is despite various prior claims that only a small fraction of the X-rays could come from CR-IC. This conclusion that CR-IC was small, in those analyses, generally depended on a few very specific assumptions which we showed are not true in the models here. (1) They assumed power-law CR-IC spectra, i.e. no CR spectral curvature. But this is never valid near the energies of interest, even for spectra extremely close to injection, and it only requires ≲Myr (< 1 kpc travel distances) for curvature to develop in arbitrarily hard pure-power-law injection spectra. (2) They assumed very hard CR spectra (often motivated by much older observations of the radio halos, or their spectral indices at either different radii or at energies which do not correspond to the same CR energies emitting CR-IC), but we find the CR spectra soften rapidly because of losses, as also required by the actual observed radio spectra at the same radii, producing much softer (and more curved)spectra thanthe softest assumed CR-IC models in previous fits. (3) Many past fits actually assumed (implicitly) that most of the X-rays were thermal, and implicitly did not allow large CR-IC, because they did things like fit out a sum of thermal components (and sometimes AGN components) and looked for residuals to this to identify as CR- IC. But this will by definition “fit out” (and classify as thermal) any CR-IC component which resembles the predicted spectra here. (4) These fits often assumed CRs were spatially smooth and uniform, so (by assumption) assumed they could not produce brightness fluctuations or multi-component spectra. But given any time-variability in the source (as observed!), or finite streaming speeds (which must be the case at the radii of interest), the natural expectation is multi-component spectra, with large-scale variability in surface brightness features very similar to those observed. We reiterate the point made in Paper III, that strictly speaking there is no X-ray measurement alone (of spectral shape or line ratios or excitation or broadening) that can rule out a significant CR-IC component of the continuum, if one allows for the full physical degrees of freedom fitting the problem (multi-phase gas with variable abundances and absorption and an arbitrary CR spectral shape, at each position). One can constrain the energetics and properties needed in the CRs in order for CR-IC to be important (as we do), but ultimately determining whether CR-IC is important or negligible requires multi-wavelength constraints of the sort we present here.

4.4. Why Don’t the 𝛾-Rays Rule Out Strong CR Pressure? As noted above, there are a number of claims in the literature that 𝛾-rays rule out ≳1% of the pressure in clusters coming from CRs. But these make several very strong and modeldependent assumptions which are not true in any of the models considered here. Specifically, they assume (1) that the CRs are entirely hadronic (most of these studies did note that leptonic CRs would be essentially invisible to the 𝛾-rays; e.g. Funk et al. 2013; Ackermann et al. 2014; Keshet 2025); (2) that CR pressure 𝑃cr varies in a specific power-law fashion with gas density according to strictly “adiabatic CR transport” (no streaming/diffusion) models (Enßlin et al. 2007; Pinzke & Pfrommer 2010), completely unlike the streaming+diffusion models here; (3) that the gas densities are much higher (using

the “apparent” values 𝑛𝑋derived from X-rays assuming no CR- IC) than they must be with significant CR-IC, which boosts the 𝛾-ray emission for a given hadronic energy density (potentially by more than an order of magnitude; see Fig. 6 and Paper III); (4) that one drops or neglects clusters with known central 𝛾-ray sources (precisely those we expect to be brightest in CR-IC), including Perseusspecifically (excludedfrom theconstraints in those studies explicitly; see Abdo et al. 2009; Huber et al. 2013; Ackermann et al. 2014; Manna & Desai 2024), because the bright central source makes it difficult or impossible to detect diffuse extended 𝛾-rays at an interesting level; and (5) that the 𝛾-ray emission comes from much larger radii ∼𝑅500 to ∼𝑅vir (see references above and Colafrancesco et al. 2010), not the central ∼100 kpc as predicted here, because the Fermi angular resolution (∼degree) corresponds to ∼Mpc scales in Perseus (and larger in more distant clusters). Dropping even one of these assumptions removes any significant tension between 𝛾- ray observations and large CR pressure in SCC centers, and clearly the models here (where none of these assumptions apply) produce strong CR pressure in the SCC center while being well below the observed 𝛾-ray limits and luminosities.

5. CONCLUSIONS We show that a simple model of CRs injected by the central radio galaxy (NGC 1275/3C 84) in Perseus can explain the observed multi-wavelength diffuse emission spectra from 106 −1026 MHz and radii ∼kpc to Mpc, specifically including the long-and-short wavelength radio, optical/UV/IR, soft and hard X-rays, and 𝛾-rays, while simultaneously reproducing independent constraints on magnetic field strengths, kinematics/dynamics/mass/potential reconstruction, “non-thermal pressure,” metallicity, and the SZ effect. As discussed for SCC clusters in general in Paper II-Paper III, as CRs propagate to ≳kpc scales, losses introduce significant curvature into the CR spectrum, which means CMB photons IC scattered by the CRs appear very similar to ∼keV thermal emission in soft X-rays, and low-frequency radio sources (dropping out of 𝛾-rays). We apply these models for the first time to an individual cluster, focusing on the best-studied and brightest X-ray SCC, Perseus. The basic scalings expected for CRs streaming from the center, plus IC emission, naturally predict the X-ray inferred or “apparent” density/temperature/entropy/pressure/cooling time/metallicity/mass-deposition rate within the SCC (≲ 100 kpc), with extended hard X-ray and 𝛾-ray emission in excellent agreement with observations. These also immediately predict the properties of the observed low-frequency radio mini-halo, including its radial surface brightness profile and spectrum from ∼20−104 MHz (and spectral evolution with radius). Notably, no re-acceleration or extended hadronic injection is necessary: the minihalo properties are predicted by the same population of streaming CRs. Future ∼10 MHz observations could test predictions here. But if we (more speculatively) extrapolate these models to the satellite population with simple scalings, we also predict a giant radio halo out to ∼Mpc scales with the observed radial profile and spectrum, coming from the contribution of many individually lower-luminosity “mini-minihalos” around each satellite galaxy in the cluster. The CR halos predicted around NGC 1275 should exist from all galaxies in the cluster, just with much lower individual luminosities/brightness, but with similar sizes ∼100 kpc (set by IC loss physics), which means their diffuse emission would overlap in a volume-filling-diffuse component which dominates over the

surviving CRs from NGC 1275 at radii ≳100 kpc, while being smoothed in time over ≳Gyr (the CR lifetime) so they do not trace current AGN but rather some much smoother time-and-population-and-space-average. If the satellites are the ultimate source of the giant halo CRs, we note that the projected surface brightness would trace the satellite distribution (as observed), the spectral index would be weakly-dependent on radius (as observed) and reflect the emission-weighted average of the younger CRs from each mini-mini-halo (also as observed), and the total giant halo luminosity (relative to NGC 1275+mini-halo) would be similar to the total satellite source injection/radio luminosity relative to NGC 1275 (∼10%, also as observed). This is distinct from some other giant radio halos which are much brighter at higher CR energies (≳GHz), as in e.g. Coma, and appear to be associated with phenomena like mergers. The CR-IC scenario, as discussed in Paper II-Paper III, provides an immediate explanation for a number of outstanding puzzles in Perseus and similar SCCs. Not only does it explain the minihalo and (potentially) giant radio halo (without any fine-tuned models for reacceleration or hadronic injection), and the quasi-universal X-ray density/entropy/pressure profiles, and the otherwise anomalous (high-temperature) harder X-ray emission, but it also naturally explains why the classical cooling flow mass deposition rate ( ¤𝑀cool ∼ 500 −1000 M⊙yr−1) is so much larger (by a factor ∼100 in Perseus) than any directly observed gas cooling or lowertemperature gas reservoir or star formation would allow, and why the apparent cooling luminosity ∼1045 erg s−1 (from ∼100 kpc) is so similar to the apparent jet/cavity power and 𝛾-ray luminosity and scales so tightly with the compact radio luminosity (from ≪kpc; see Paper III for details). These are all just different manifestations of the same leptonic source, rather than some fine-tuned balance between thermal cooling and AGN heating. It also explains the observed deviations between mass/potential models and metallicities estimated via X-rays versus other methods at radii well inside the SCC (≪100 kpc).

5.1. Model Assumptions & Differences from Previous Models The key assumptions in our models are:

• The total effective leptonic injection rate ¤𝐸cr, ℓfrom the NGC 1275 AGN+jet+cavity system is something like ∼1045 erg s−1, as indicated by standard models of the compact radio core, jets, AGN and 𝛾-rays (Böttcher et al. 2013; Tavecchio & Ghisellini 2014; Keenan et al. 2021; Hodgson et al. 2021; Foschini et al. 2024).

• The magnetic field in the volume-filling, X-ray emitting gas at ∼100 kpc is something like 0.5 −5 𝜇G, as indicated by present upper and lower limits (from RMs, kinematics, and prior radio+X-ray constraints; § 3.5.3 & Fig. 18; Taylor et al. 2006; Sanders & Fabian 2007; Hitomi Collaboration et al. 2018b; Svensmark et al. 2021; van Weeren et al. 2024; Creech et al. 2024; Kam et al. 2026).

• The “effective” transport speeds (𝑣st + 𝑣adv + 𝜅/𝑅+ ...) for CRs are something like ∼40 −200 km s−1 at ∼GV in the diffuse gas at ∼100 kpc, order-of-magnitude similar to observed values in the ISM and CGM (Karwin et al. 2019; Recchia et al. 2021; Butsky et al. 2023;

Hopkins et al. 2025c), as well as observed buoyant/bulk transport speeds within the SCC (Hitomi Collaboration et al. 2018a; Kempski et al. 2023; Hlavacek-Larrondo & Perseus Team / Xrism Collaboration 2025), and within an factor of a few of their Alfvén speeds.

With these conditions met, we have shown that most of our qualitative predictions are not extremely sensitive to the details of the underlying “true” 𝐵, 𝑛, 𝑇, or 𝑍, the source/injection spectrum of injection/acceleration volume, how exactly the transport speeds scale with radius or plasma properties, or the presence of turbulent reacceleration or streaming losses. Where they are more sensitive, these parameters often enter in a degenerate fashion, so with modest exploration of parameter space many distinct but qualitatively similar solutions are plausible. As discussed in detail in § 4, these assumptions explain why (1) turbulent re-acceleration is neither necessary nor significant in the models here, to explain the radio mini-halo (and even giant halo); (2) previous claims of strong upper limits IC in X-rays (soft and hard), which assumed qualitatively different CR spectra than the models above predict, could not distinguish the extremely thermal-like CR-IC spectra predicted; and (3) prior claims of limits to non-thermal pressure (from 𝛾- rays or turbulent or kinematic constraints) do not apply to the models here (and those measurements are well-reproduced). We stress that we considered intentionally extremely-simple models. We assumed spherical symmetry, time-steady-state with a constant ¤𝐸cr, ℓ, constant 𝜅and 𝑣st in space and time, and simple empirical fits for the gas properties. If we relaxed these assumptions, it gives many new degrees of freedom. For example, given a more realistic time-and-space variable CR injection rate and CR transport physics, one expects a multiage distribution of CRs to reside at a given radius (just like one would expect more than a single gas temperature in a multiphase gas system). We could then fit the observed spectra to effective “multi-temperature CR-IC” plus multi-temperature gas models (effectively, fitting a model for the best-fit CR spectrum plus gas phases as a function of position to the X-ray and radio multi-wavelength maps simultaneously). Given the similarity of the simple models here to the observed spectra already, and the already-known degeneracies fitting multi-wavelength and/or multi-component spectra to any of these datasets (see Matsushita et al. 2002; Mazzotta et al. 2004; Avestruz et al. 2014; Vĳayan & Li 2022; ZuHone et al. 2023), it is almost trivially guaranteed that one could find formally “good fits” throughout Perseus with such an approach. The problem is that fitting the true degrees-of-freedom we expect (a multicomponent CR spectrum with arbitrary spectral curvature and sum-of-components plus a multi-phase gas distribution with arbitrary temperature and density distributions) is highly degenerate, so the best fit solutions would almost certainly be non-unique.

5.2. Alternative Models and Future Work We emphasize that nothing we have argued strictly rules out the “traditional” (no CR-IC) interpretation of the Perseus SCC, but it is challenging to reconcile the full ensemble of observations with that scenario for reasons we review here. The cleanest way to recover that limit is to make the following assumptions. (1) Assume order-of-magnitude faster CR transport speeds 𝑣st ≫1000 km s−1 outside the AGN (the CR source luminosity of NGC 1275 must be broadly similar to explain the AGN and 𝛾-ray properties), so that CRs escape rapidly and

maintain a much lower 𝑒cr and therefore much weaker CR-IC (Fig. 4-9). (2) To explain the radio with much lower 𝑒cr, assume factor of ≳5−10 stronger magnetic fields 𝐵everywhere. This will create tension with observed Faraday rotation measurements (one must assume that, despite being measured in the sub-pc radio core, the RMs measured actually come from gas at ∼100 kpc, with plasma 𝛽∼1 around the mini-halo radius ∼100 kpc; see Fig. 18), and with the non-thermal pressure upper limits from potential/hydrostatic/kinematic constraints, but these tensions are not impossible to reconcile. (3) Reintroduce strong re-acceleration to explain the giant radio halo (Fig. 13). This would require something like 𝜅being very low, despite streaming speeds 𝑣st being very large, so the CR transport would have to be some unusual form of sub-diffusion or advection. On top of this, without CR-IC, there is of course the usual cooling flow problem in the X-rays with 99% of the apparent cooling luminosity at ∼100 −200 kpc being offset by an AGN at ≪1 kpc without producing much visible cooling; some other physics must explain how the CF sets up the quasi-universal apparent soft-X-ray density 𝑛𝑋and temperature 𝑇𝑋profiles; additional new physics like dust depletion (i.e. large dust populations in ∼108 K gas) must be invoked to explain why the X-ray-inferred metallicities 𝑍𝑋are suppressed relative to UV/optical metallicities at ≪100 kpc (Fig. 8; Panagoulia et al. 2015; Liu et al. 2019; Ng & Ueda 2024); the “intermediate” hard X-ray components require a small, undetected-at-other wavelengths component of highly super-virial ∼20 −60 keV gas (Fig. 9); reacceleration models must be fine-tuned (fitting numbers like 𝜅(𝑅)) to give the correct halo extent while also explaining why the radio spectrum softens from 1−100 kpc instead of hardening (the expectation for a re-acceleration-dominated spectrum; § 4.2); and different physics such as shocks must be invoked to explain the higher-frequency component and/or giant halo, whose similarity to the galaxy profile observed is coincidental in this case (Fig. 16); and the observed strong deviations of the central kinematics and X-ray mass/potential reconstruction must still imply the gas is highly out-of-hydrostatic equilibrium, but in this case without any other source of pressure (Fig. 19). All of this is, in principle, still plausible. But an appealing aspect of the CR-IC models here is that all of this phenomenology instead has a single, simple physical explanation. In a companion paper, we will investigate another prediction of the models here: ionization and excitation of neutral (atomic/molecular) gas within the apparent SCC. Owing to the large implied CR “bath” in the models here, strong ionization and excitation is predicted, and indeed this is observed (Johnstone et al. 2007; Ferland et al. 2008, 2009; Salomé et al. 2011; Vantyghem et al. 2017), consistent with the other observational phenomena discussed here, and challenging to understand in a model without significant CR-IC. Perseus is typical of many SCC clusters, but there are regimes where we might expect qualitatively different behaviors. First is at high redshifts. Because the CMB energy density scales ∝(1 + 𝑧)4, if CR streaming speeds are universal/constant and injection is leptonic (streaming and diffusing from a central source), then CR-IC halos would become systematically brighter in the emission frame (similar brightness observed), but also more compact, at higher-redshift, with the effects becoming potentially noticeable as early as 𝑧≳0.5−1 or so. This could be very important for the extreme SCCs known at intermediate redshifts, like H1821+643 and

the Phoenix cluster (Walker et al. 2014; McDonald et al. 2019), 𝑧≳1 (e.g. 3C 186, SPT J2215+3537, and others; Siemiginowska et al. 2010; Santos et al. 2012; Ghirardini et al. 2021; Calzadilla et al. 2023), and even 𝑧≳2 (Spiderweb, IDCS J1426.5+3508, MQN01, XLSSC 122; Brodwin et al. 2016; Mantz et al. 2018; Lepore et al. 2024; Travascio et al. 2025; Duffy et al. 2022) which seem to show very high-surfacebrightness SCCs (comparable brightness observed independent of redshift, as predicted for CR-IC, see Paper III) with sometimes sharp edges and apparent gradients in X-ray properties (like 𝑍𝑋) and more compact central peaks at the highest redshifts (see Paper III). At the opposite extreme are WCCs, including systems like Virgo and Centaurus (as well as smaller groups like HGC 62). These have orders-of-magnitude lower X-ray inferred cooling and mass deposition rates than Perseus, and show essentially no evidence for any neutral or multi-phase gas within the SCC at any radii outside the BCG nucleus (≳1 kpc; Salomé et al. 2016; Boselli et al. 2019; Boizelle et al. 2025). But they still appear to show some of the signs of a CR-IC “boosted” CC: they have strong central radio sources (albeit orders-ofmagnitude less luminous than NGC 1275); their central X-rayinferred metallicities are much smaller than those measured in UV/optical at the same radii (Russell et al. 2018; XRISM Collaboration et al. 2025); they show an apparent rising X-ray surface brightness (Churazov et al. 2008; McCall et al. 2024); and they have ultra-steep radio “mini-mini-halos” around the BCG (Mtshweni 2022; Wu et al. 2025; de Gasperin et al. 2025). This suggests similar CR processes may be occurring there too, but at an overall reduced level.

5.3. Future Observational Tests We have attempted to compile extensive multi-wavelength Perseus diffuse-gas measurements, to test the models here. Of course, future measurements could further constrain and inform the models here, and potentially definitively rule in or out proposals here like the role of CR-IC in X-ray emission, aging CRs in the minihalo, or satellite mini-mini halos contributing to the giant halo. Here we summarize the most straightforward tests proposed in the text.

1. Better spatial and spectral-resolved X-ray measurements that can obtain detailed de-projected multi-phase (multi-𝑍𝑋, 𝑇𝑋) measurements well within the SCC, of the sort possible with future instruments like ATHENA, could be very constraining if coupled to new independent measurements of gas-phase 𝑍≈𝑍true from non Xray (radio/IR/optical/UV) measurements. Gas clearly exists out to ≳30 kpc in phases (ionized ∼104−5 K, neutral, molecular) where such measurements are conceivable. The variant models here differ widely in their predicted behaviors for 𝑍𝑋given some true 𝑍true, so this combination is particularly powerful for breaking those degeneracies, with 𝑍𝑋(𝑅) ≲𝑍true(𝑅) strongly favoring significant non-thermal emission.

2. Spatially-resolved low-frequency radio at ∼1−20 MHz would enable one to directly probe the same electrons responsible for X-ray CR-IC. The X-rays are sensitive to the spectrum of ∼0.3 −2 GeV leptons, while current radio with required spatial resolution and sensitivity (to map diffuse emission within the core, away from the jets/lobes) corresponds to ∼4 −30 GeV leptons (while reaching ∼1 −20 MHz would probe ∼1 GeV leptons).

Then one could directly ask whether the spectral shapes are potentially consistent with CR-IC contributing significantly to the X-ray continuum, and how the local variations in emissivity do or do not correlate within the diffuse CC gas. To avoid significant CR-IC emission, while reproducing existing radio, there would need to be a sharp cutoff in the radio spectrum between those frequencies and the frequencies already observed (e.g. just below ∼70 MHz).

3. As noted above, a pure-thermal X-ray explanation would require larger gas densities and order-of-magnitude larger 𝐵≳10 𝜇G within the outer CC (∼30−100 kpc), in order to still explain the radio (for any reasonable CR spectrum). As such, independent Faraday rotation measurements from background sources, like fast radio bursts (FRBs), with impact parameters within the inner CC ≪100 kpc of Perseus, would be especially valuable. Given the gas density profiles implied by the standard pure-thermal fits, plus the minimum 𝐵required to reproduce the radio mini-halo spectrum, pure-thermal models would imply |RM(𝑅∼30−80 kpc)| ≳30, 000 rad m−2. Upper limits to RMs below this would strongly favor ACRH models like those here, and detections or upper limits below ≲1000 rad m−2, like the ≲110 rad m−2 found in the one measured FRB RM in a cluster (in Abell 2311; Connor et al. 2023), would definitively rule out “thermal only” models for the soft X-rays (given the observed radio and hard X-rays). Lacking background sources, improved measurements of the spatial and temporal variability of RMs from the cluster radio core and jets can improve the RM upper limits from the diffuse gas (with the upper limit from diffuse gas at ≫kpc corresponding to the minimum RMs measured in spaceand-time across the jets being monitored). In Virgo, for example, this has shown that the RM from the diffuse CC gas must be ≲130 rad m−2 (Park et al. 2019), an order of magnitude smaller than the contribution from the (rapidly space-and-time varying) jet core+sheath.

4. Future SZ measurements resolving the CC would provide a very clear and robust distinguishing method between models with significant CR-IC (more low-energy leptons) and those without, and place a robust prior on the true thermal pressure 𝑃true ≈𝑃SZ. As discussed above however, this is challenging, as it requires a combination of high resolution and dramatic improvements in sidelobe control to avoid contamination by the core of NGC 1275. Future samples of fast radio burst (FRB) or dispersion measure (DM) measurements probing the central CC could accomplish the same (measuring the true column 𝑁H, true) without contamination concerns.

5. Future high-energy constraints from 𝛾-rays and very hard X-rays can also be a powerful constraint. However especially for 𝛾-rays, which could most strongly constrain the hadron-to-lepton ratios, or leptonic spectrum near ∼GeV, directly testing the predictions here would require orders-of-magnitude improvements in angular resolution (to few-arcsecond) and background control/extended low-surface brightness sensitivity (ideally a factor ∼200 −1000 improvement over GeV Fermi backgrounds), with peak sensitivity between ∼10 −1000 MeV. 6. Measurements of CR ionization of dense atomic/molecular gas within the cooling filamentary structure in the Perseus CC can provide a powerful and unique bolometer of the pressure and number density of precisely the low-energy CRs that matter for CR-IC and for the ACRH and aging diffuse synchrotron minihalo. As noted above, making quantitative predictions for these measurements will be the subject of future work (in preparation).

All of these represent important future topics for study.

# The Virgo Cluster as a Case Study for Ancient Cosmic Ray Halos in Radio and X-rays

**Authors:** Philip F. Hopkins1∗ Emily M. Silich1 Jack Sayers1 Sam B. Ponnada1 Isabel S. Sands1 Affiliation: 1Division of Physics, Mathematics, and Astronomy, California Institute of Technology, Pasadena, CA 91125, USA Affiliation: 2Department of Astrophysical Sciences, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ 08544, USA

## Abstract

Virgo is the nearest cool core (CC) galaxy cluster, and is archetypal of the class of X-ray weak CCs. Despite the X-ray continuum implying a large cooling rate ( $\gtrsim 10\,{\rm M_{\odot}\,yr^{-1}}$ ), measurements of cooler gas phases, dust, and star formation show almost no cooling outside the M87 nucleus. It is also known that M87∗ is a prodigious source of cosmic ray (CR) leptons observed in radio and $\gamma$ -rays, and recent radio observations have shown that the M87 radio halo is low-frequency and its spectral index steepens rapidly away from the injection region+jets, consistent with an aging, low-energy CR population. We demonstrate that coupling X-ray and radio to newer Faraday rotation limits on the magnetic field, this implies the CRs within the CC radius ( $\lesssim 40$ kpc) must contribute significantly to the total pressure and soft X-ray emission, through a combination of Coulomb heating the gas and inverse-Compton (IC) scattering microwave background photons to $\sim$ keV. We show this can explain the apparent correspondence between jet/radio power and X-ray cooling luminosity, and why the X-ray inferred cooling rate appears much larger than otherwise observed. This would also explain why the central X-ray inferred metallicity at $\lesssim 10\,$ kpc appears to be suppressed relative to the UV/optical inferred metallicity (in a wavelength-dependent manner). Compared to more extreme radio+X-ray sources like Perseus, we find the observations require a softer “escaping” CR spectrum (escaping or accelerated outside $\gtrsim 1\,$ kpc from M87∗).

#### keywords

## 1 Introduction

“Cool core” (CC) clusters have been the subject of intense study in astrophysics for their implications in galaxy formation, ICM/CGM plasma physics, and supermassive black hole (BH) or active galactic nucleus (AGN) “feedback” and the quenching of star formation (McNamara and Nulsen, 2007, e.g.). While X-ray luminous “strong cool cores” (SCCs) like Perseus have received much of the attention in this field, owing to their extreme properties (e.g. apparent X-ray cooling luminosities in excess of $\sim 10^{45}\,{\rm erg\,s^{-1}}$ ), it is important to note that the overwhelming majority of CCs by number, and the vast majority of the population-and-redshift integrated X-ray “cooling luminosity” in the Universe, comes from much less-extreme but more common “weak cool core” (WCC) systems (Reiprich and Böhringer, 2002; Peres et al., 1998; Mittal et al., 2011a; Koens et al., 2013; Böhringer, Hans et al., 2014; Pacaud et al., 2016; Hopkins et al., 2026b). Archetypes of the WCC category in the local Universe include clusters like Virgo, Centaurus, Ophiuchus, and groups like NGC 5044 and HGC 62. In these systems the classically-inferred X-ray cooling luminosity $L_{X,\,{\rm cool}}$ of gas with an inferred cooling time $\lesssim 7\,$ Gyr is more like $\sim 10^{43}\,{\rm erg\,s^{-1}}$ , and the implied “mass deposition rate” that should be occurring owing to the cooling is $\dot{M}_{X,\,{\rm cool}}\sim 10\,{\rm M_{\odot}\,yr^{-1}}$ , interior to an apparent “cooling radius” $R_{X,\,{\rm cool}}$ of order $\sim 20-40\,$ kpc (Cavagnolo et al., 2009; Hudson et al., 2010; Mittal et al., 2011a; Liu et al., 2024). The classical “cooling flow” (CF) problem in these clusters is defined by the fact that they show little to no evidence for any such cooling. Although in SCCs like Perseus there is almost always some significant multi-phase gas, in WCCs like the specific clusters above, the upper limits to the neutral, warm ionized ( $\lesssim 10^{6}\,$ K), molecular, and dust masses are typically $\lesssim 10^{5}-10^{7}\,{\rm M_{\odot}}$ outside of the galactic nuclei deep within the ISM of the BCG (central couple kpc; see Valluri and Anupama 1996; Gallagher et al. 2008; Mittal et al. 2011b; Hoffer et al. 2012; Sparks et al. 2012; Hamer et al. 2012; Werner et al. 2013; Werner et al. 2014; di Serego Alighieri et al. 2013; Salomé et al. 2016; Lakhchaura et al. 2018; Boselli et al. 2019; Olivares et al. 2019; Rose et al. 2019; Richtler et al. 2020). And their past Gyr-averaged star formation rates (SFRs) $\dot{M}_{\ast}$ are robustly constrained by a combination of UV, optical, and infrared spectroscopic observations plus (in cases like M87 in Virgo) additional novae and supernovae rates, (lack of) young star clusters or high-mass X-ray binaries, to be $\dot{M}_{\ast}\lesssim 0.1-0.2\,{\rm M_{\odot}\,yr^{-1}}$ .11 1 More recent analyses of the central regions of M87 have argued that nova rates (Matteucci et al., 2003; Lessing et al., 2024), resolved CMDs (Cook et al., 2020), and UV spectra (Tamhane et al., 2025) place a much more stringent $\lesssim 10^{-4}\,{\rm M_{\odot}\,yr^{-1}}$ upper limit on the recent star formation rate. Meanwhile previous claims of molecular gas detections even at sub-kpc scales appear to be dominated by contamination or intervening structures not associated with M87, with upper limits on the total molecular gas mass now revised to $\ll 10^{5}\,{\rm M_{\odot}}$ , with maximum molecular surface density $\lesssim 1\,{\rm M_{\odot}\,pc^{-2}}$ in the central $<100\,$ pc (Kawanaka et al., 2025; Boizelle et al., 2025).

There are other puzzles as well. For example, in all of the above clusters, the inferred metallicity from X-ray spectra (fit to single-temperature models) of the central $\lesssim 1-10\,$ kpc appear to be shockingly low, $Z_{X}(R\ll 1-10\,{\rm kpc})\sim 0.1-0.3\,Z_{\odot}$ (Böhringer et al., 2001; Molendi and Gastaldello, 2001; Matsushita et al., 2002; Churazov et al., 2008; Russell et al., 2015; Russell et al., 2018), but for the same radii and galaxies there are robust measurements of both gas-phase and stellar-phase metallicities from standard UV/optical/near-IR diagnostics that all show similar modestly-super-Solar ( $Z_{\rm opt/UV/NIR}\sim 1.5-2\,Z_{\odot}$ ) metallicities (Olivares et al., 2025, e.g.). And the X-ray inferred “hydrostatic equilibrium” mass profiles interior to $\lesssim 10\,$ kpc appear (in more modern, more accurate measurements) to disagree by factors of several with the mass profiles from a combination of stellar and gas and globular cluster kinematics (Das et al., 2010; Murphy et al., 2011; Agnello et al., 2014; Liepold et al., 2023).

Moreover, the small CCs of these halos also show – at the same radii – low-frequency radio halos. In Virgo, for example, within the central $\sim 20-40\,$ kpc around M87 there is diffuse, volume-filling radio emission detected by LOFAR and other instruments at frequencies as low as $20\,$ MHz (Owen et al., 2000; de Gasperin et al., 2012; Edler et al., 2023; de Gasperin et al., 2025). While clearly powered by the famous BH at the center of M87 and its associated jets, the diffuse spectrum is now seen to be (1) very steep even at $\sim 10\,$ kpc from the radio core or jet termination shocks, and (2) to steepen rapidly with increasing distance from those source regions, with most of the diffuse halo volume showing an “ultra steep” spectrum with very clear spectral curvature. Indeed the high-frequency portion of the spectrum appears to steepen to spectral indices as steep as $\alpha\sim 2.5-4$ before becoming undetectable at $\gtrsim 10\,$ kpc, where the lowest-frequency halo persists to larger radii comparable to the CC (Rottmann et al., 1996; de Gasperin et al., 2012; Mtshweni, 2022; Wu et al., 2025). This requires a large population of diffuse, low-energy cosmic rays (CRs).

In Hopkins et al. (2025b), we suggested that many puzzles in CCs like those above could be naturally explained by “ancient” cosmic ray halos (ACRHs) within the CC. CR leptons accelerated by the radio galaxy stream outwards, but the high-energy ( $E_{\rm cr}\gg$ GeV) CRs rapidly lose their energy, leaving a population with energy at $\sim 0.1-1\,$ GeV which simultaneously explain the low-frequency radio halo and inverse-Compton (IC) scatter CMB photons to $\sim$ 1 keV energies, producing a remarkably thermal-continuum-like soft X-ray spectrum (Hopkins et al., 2025a) with substantial curvature (owing to the curvature of the CR spectrum imprinted by losses). These CR-IC X-ray halos dim as they stream out but can reach $\sim 100\,$ kpc before losing all their energy. In Hopkins et al. (2026b), we showed that these ACRHs would naturally explain a number of properties of CCs, including their characteristic “universal” X-ray inferred surface brightness (SB) and density/temperature/pressure/entropy profiles, and alleviate the CF problem because the X-ray continuum is boosted by CR-IC (so the true cooling luminosity can be much lower). We showed they also trivially explain the various observed correlations between AGN/radio/jet/cavity power and $L_{X,\,{\rm cool}}$ , as both trace the same lepton population; as well as other properties like the CC size-luminosity relation. Hopkins et al. (2026a), henceforth Paper I, applied these models to a detailed case study of Perseus, as archetypal of SCCs, and showed that the expected ACRH from the BCG (NGC 1275/3C 84, with leptonic injection rate $\sim 10^{45}\,{\rm erg\,s^{-1}}$ ) can explain the spatially-and-spectrally observed properties from radio ( $\gtrsim 10\,$ MHz) through soft and hard X-ray and $\gamma$ -ray ( $\lesssim$ TeV) from $R\sim 1-100\,$ kpc within the apparent SCC. And Hopkins et al. (2025c) showed the associated low-energy CR population naturally explains the otherwise extremely puzzling high-excitation properties of the neutral atomic and molecular gas in the diffuse SCC (distances $\gtrsim 10\,$ kpc from the BCG, with excitation more similar to gas observed in strong CR environments like pulsar wind nebulae, e.g. the Crab, as compared to the local interstellar medium [LISM]; Ferland et al. 2008; Salomé et al. 2011; Bayet et al. 2011; Canning et al. 2016). Given the broadly similar but quantitatively distinct puzzles above, associated with WCCs, it seems important to consider if the same models, scaled to the properties of a typical WCC halo and BCG like M87, can explain a similar range of phenomena.

In this paper, we therefore apply these same ACRH models from Paper I (with appropriately rescaled properties) to the best-studied WCC, Virgo. We show that a simple model, assuming M87∗ accelerates $\sim 10^{43}\,{\rm erg\,s^{-1}}$ of CR leptons, can explain the apparent WCC X-ray apparent SB/density/temperature/pressure/entropy/mass deposition rate/cooling luminosity interior to the CC (while remaining below hard X-ray and $\gamma$ -ray upper limits) and the radio “mini-minihalo” spectrum from $\sim 10-10^{3}\,$ MHz and radial profile out to $\sim 40\,$ kpc. It can also potentially explain the discrepancy between X-ray and NIR/optical/UV-inferred metallicities at $\sim 1\,$ kpc. § 2 summarizes the model and changed inputs from Paper I. § 3 shows the resulting predictions for X-ray properties/profiles, metallicities, the central radio profile, and high energy constraints, as well as SZ and kinematic/mass/potential models. § 5 summarizes and discusses these results.

## 2 Model

We consider a simple analytic model defined in Paper I. Specifically, we adopt a spherically symmetric cluster with a specified diffuse/volume-filling gas density $n$ , temperature $T$ , metallicity $Z$ , mass $M(<r)$ , and magnetic field $B$ profile, with CRs obeying the steady-state, spherically-symmetric Fokker Planck equation:

$$ \displaystyle 0 \displaystyle=\frac{1}{r^{2}}\frac{\partial}{\partial r}\left[r^{2}\left(\kappa\,\frac{\partial f}{\partial r}-v_{\rm st}f\right)\right]+\frac{\partial(p\mathcal{R}f)}{\partial p}+S(r,p)\ . $$

in terms of an effective diffusivity $\kappa$ , streaming speed $v_{\rm st}$ (which includes Alfvénic or diffusive-like “super-Alfvénic” streaming, or super-diffusion, or advection/convective transport), losses $\mathcal{R}$ , and source term $S$ . The source term is treated as a point-like injection in a sphere at $R<1\,$ kpc – what we refer to here as the “injection zone”: we only evolve the CRs outside of $>1\,$ kpc, since we are only interested in the diffuse gas and CRs, not the inner AGN/jets/lobes/etc. or acceleration mechanisms. Thus what matters is the spectrum emerging from these radii. For background properties we adopt simple fits to the properties at large radii and constraints from non X-ray observations, extrapolated to the central regions as if for a non-cool-core cluster: $(n/{\rm cm^{-3}})^{2}=n^{2}_{0}\,(r/r_{c})^{-a_{0}}\,\{[1+(r/r_{c})^{2}]^{(3\,a_{1}-a_{0})/2}[1+(r/r_{s})^{3}]^{a_{2}/3}\}^{-1}$ with $(r_{c},\,r_{s},r_{500},\,a_{0},\,a_{1},\,a_{2},\,n_{0})=(0.04\,r_{500},\,0.6\,r_{500},660\,{\rm kpc},\,0.5,\,0.35,\,2.6,\,0.005)$ ; $k_{B}T/{\rm keV}=3.6\,\{1+(r/0.7\,r_{500})^{2}+(r/r_{500})^{10}\}^{-0.3}$ ; $Z/Z_{\odot}=0.1+[0.5+r/r_{c}]^{-1}$ ; $(B/{\rm\mu G})^{-2}=[0.1+50\,{\rm kpc}/r]^{-2}+15^{-2}$ , and $M(<r)$ corresponding to the sum of a central isothermal sphere profile with $V_{c}=500\,{\rm km\,s^{-1}}$ plus an NFW profile with $M_{\rm vir}=1.5\times 10^{14}\,M_{\odot}$ and concentration $c_{\rm vir}=7.5$ . We stress that the details of these profiles are not important to our conclusions: all that matters is that they give us a plausible fit to larger-radii behavior, while intentionally extrapolating to values below the X-ray inferred $n_{X}$ in the cluster center, and giving a plausible radio profile from e.g. $B$ and the CR models we will study (for example, considering a halo more massive by factors $\sim 5-7$ , per § 3.5, has no effect on our predictions). We take the diffuse radiation field at each $r$ , needed to calculate IC effects, to be given by the sum of the metagalactic backgrounds+CMB compiled from Cooray (2016); Khaire and Srianand (2019), plus the observed M87 starlight+dust spectrum from far-IR through EUV, plus the compact M87∗ radio+ $\gamma$ -ray spectrum, assuming this decreases as $\propto 1/r^{2}$ (compiled from NED and Berghöfer et al. 1999; Bonamente et al. 2001; Kormendy et al. 2009; Rudick et al. 2010; Krick et al. 2011 in Alfaro et al. 2022 and shown in § 3.4), plus the emitted thermal gas-cooling (primarily X-ray) plus CR emission (radio+X-ray+ $\gamma$ -ray) predicted (like Paper I, this means we iterate the models, calculating the initial emission, then using this to update the radiation fields seen by CRs, re-calculating the CR emission spectrum, and so forth, until convergence).

For the CRs we adopt a leptonic injection rate $\dot{E}_{\rm cr}=\int_{0}^{\infty}\int_{0}^{\infty}4\pi r^{2}S\,drdp=3\times 10^{43}\,{\rm erg\,s^{-1}}$ , motivated by direct observations and modeling of the M87∗ core radio and high-energy $\gamma$ -ray emission spectrum and variability, which argue for leptonic injection rates in the range $\sim 4-10\times 10^{43}\,{\rm erg\,s^{-1}}$ (e.g. Honda and Honda, 2007; Alfaro et al., 2022; Hakobyan et al., 2025, and references therein). Since our injection zone is the central kpc of M87, which has conditions similar to the local ISM through which the CRs must have already propagated and been processed, we assume a default leptonic injection-zone spectrum following the observed LISM lepton spectrum from Bisschoff et al. (2019), as in Hopkins et al. (2025a); Hopkins et al. (2025b); Hopkins et al. (2026b). This is also consistent with the spectrum that would emerge from many processes, such as pure power-law injection with a slope $d\dot{N}/dp\propto p^{-2.2}$ after processing in the central kpc by synchrotron and inverse-Compton losses, or initially “hadronic” injection by pionic processes from an initially hadronic CR spectrum traveling through a dense column on sub-kpc scales (although Atoyan and Dermer 2003 and Alfaro et al. 2022 argue a hadronic jet would require an unrealistic $>10^{50}\,{\rm erg\,s^{-1}}$ injection power, and H. E. S. S. Collaboration et al. 2023 place upper limits on the hadronic mass escaping into the cluster). For simplicity we adopt a constant in space-and-time $\kappa=10^{28}\,{\rm cm^{2}\,s^{-1}}\,f(E_{\rm cr})$ and $v_{\rm st}=100\,{\rm km\,s^{-1}}\,f(E_{\rm cr})$ , with $f(E_{\rm cr})\sim 1+(E_{\rm cr}/{\rm GeV})^{1/2}$ consistent with standard fits from codes like GALPROP/DRAGON2/PICARD/USINE as well as CR-MHD simulations in the LISM (Weinrich et al., 2020; Zhao et al., 2021; Hopkins et al., 2022a; Hopkins et al., 2022b; Korsmeier and Cuoco, 2022; Di Mauro et al., 2024; Jacobs et al., 2023; Silver and Orlando, 2024; De La Torre Luque and Linden, 2024; Tovar-Pardo et al., 2024; Ramírez et al., 2024; Recchia and Gabici, 2024). Like in Paper I, we have considered variations to all of the above choices. Some have almost no effect on our most of our predictions (e.g. $M(<r)$ , or $n(r)$ at small radii, which is only important for the very-central metallicity profile predicted, shown in § 3.2). Some, like $B$ , are allowed to have a wide range of values (shown in § 3.5.1), with the default choice here chosen in all cases to be the most “conservative” (the one for which it is least-trivial to explain X-ray properties via CR-IC), but these are effectively degenerate with other choices like the shape of the injection spectrum for some properties (like the radio spectrum in the central $\lesssim 10\,$ kpc). The shape of the injection spectrum only matters very close to the injection zone, as shown in Hopkins et al. (2026a); Hopkins et al. (2025b); Hopkins et al. (2026b); Hopkins et al. (2025a); Hopkins et al. (2025c) and Paper I, as the combination of Coulomb+synchrotron+IC losses very quickly force it to converge to a universal shape, so one should treat the predictions at the smallest radii as more sensitive to these choices, while the predictions at $R\gtrsim 10\,$ kpc are more robust. The total injection luminosity of course just scales the predictions up/down accordingly. There is also some degeneracy between the values of $\kappa$ and $v_{\rm st}$ , and whether we assume these are energy-dependent or not, as in the LISM, and we discuss this in § 4.

The important point is that this is a simple choice of a “fiducial” model, and as should be obvious many of the values we adopt for parameters are simply an approximate “round number” – these are not in any way fitted to the observations. In fact in exploring the parameter space we find other model choices which slightly better-fit some of the observational datasets to which we compare (but we stay with the fiducial values as those shown, because of their simplicity). But like in Paper I, there are many model variants that fit the observations comparably well, especially owing to partial parameter degeneracies. The variations and their effects are shown therein – here we choose to show just a single fiducial model for clarity, because it illustrates the key point, that a simple model for CR-IC can plausibly explain a wealth of multi-wavelength observations.

## 3 Results

The key predictions from these models, and their comparison to observations, are presented here, at wavelengths from $10^{6}-10^{26}$ Hz, and cluster-centric radii $\sim 1-1000\,$ kpc.

### 3.1 Cosmic Ray Spectra

Fig. 1 shows CR spectra at different spherical radii $r$ in mock cluster, evolved as above. As in our previous ACRH studies (Hopkins et al., 2026a; Hopkins et al., 2025b; Hopkins et al., 2026b; Hopkins et al., 2025a), the CR spectra exhibit a high degree of curvature, and converge rapidly outside of $\sim 1-10\,$ kpc to the same form as they are shaped by a combination of Coulomb losses (rapid at low energies) and synchrotron+IC losses (rapid at high energies). Critically, over any non-negligible baseline in energy, they are poorly approximated by power-law spectra $dN_{\rm cr}/dE_{\rm cr}\propto E_{\rm cr}^{-\delta}$ , and especially poorly approximated by the common assumption $\delta\sim 2.2$ often invoked in searches for IC emission. As shown in those papers above, for CR spectra peaked, like these, at $\sim 0.1-1\,$ GeV, there are three peaks in the direct CR emission: $\sim$ MHz radio synchrotron, $\sim$ keV soft X-ray IC, and $\sim 10-100\,$ MeV $\gamma$ -ray bremsstrahlung.

### 3.2 Soft X-ray

Fig. 2 shows the soft X-ray properties versus radius from the model. We show the (projected 2D) surface brightness in a corrected $0.1-10\,$ keV band, and the de-projected (3D) profile of the X-ray inferred density $n_{X}$ , temperature $T_{X}$ , and metallicity $Z_{X}$ which reproduce the same emissivity, spectral shape/hardness, and Fe K line equivalent width, as the modeled CR-IC + thermal APEC spectrum at each radius (see Paper I for details). We also present various derived X-ray properties including entropy $K_{X}\equiv k_{B}T_{X}/n_{X}^{2/3}$ , pressure $P_{X}\equiv n_{X}k_{B}T_{X}$ , cooling time $t_{{\rm cool},\,X}\equiv(3/2)\,n_{X}\,k_{B}\,T_{X}/n_{X}^{2}\Lambda(T_{X},\,Z_{X})$ , and cooling or mass deposition rate $\dot{M}_{X}\equiv\int(2\mu m_{p}/5k_{B}T_{X})dL_{{\rm cool},\,X}(r)$ . For each, we also show the “true” (thermal-only) background properties assumed in the model. We compile and compare X-ray observations from Böhringer et al. (2001); Matsushita et al. (2002); Young et al. (2002); Churazov et al. (2008); Urban et al. (2011); Russell et al. (2015); Russell et al. (2018); Simionescu et al. (2017); McCall et al. (2024); XRISM Collaboration et al. (2025), from XMM, Chandra, Suzaku, eROSITA, and XRISM. Where possible, because we are interested in the diffuse emission, we show the interquartile range along different sightlines/azimuthal angles/pixels at the same $r$ observed.

We stress that the models here are not fit to the observations: we simply tried a few parameters as described in § 2 and show a plausible example. And they are extremely simple (spherically-symmetric, point-like LISM-like injection, time-steady, constant- $v_{\rm st}$ and $\kappa$ , etc.), and as such actually involve significantly fewer parameters than the commonly-adopted fitting functions from e.g. Vikhlinin (2006) for $n_{X}$ , $T_{X}$ , $P_{X}$ , $K_{X}$ , etc. Thus the resemblance to the observations is highly non-trivial.

#### 3.2.1 Alleviating the Cooling Flow Problem & Explaining the AGN-Halo Connection

The model in Fig. 2 provides an immediate explanation for the classical-versus-spectral cooling flow problem, defined by the apparent classical cooling rate from the X-ray continuum being at least two orders of magnitude larger than the upper limits on actual cooling from a combination of X-ray spectroscopy, infrared dust surveys, HI surveys, radio molecular gas surveys, UV star formation diagnostics, and more (see § 1). Because CR-IC boosts the apparent X-ray SB and therefore $n_{X}$ , it boosts $L_{X}$ while decreasing $t_{\rm cool}$ , greatly increasing the apparent $\dot{M}_{X}$ below some cooling time threshold (here the usual $7$ Gyr adopted), as compared to the true cooling rate of the gas. Per Hopkins et al. (2025b); Hopkins et al. (2026b), this also provides an almost-trivial explanation for the apparent close relationship between the apparent X-ray cooling luminosity $L_{{\rm cool},\,X}\sim 10^{43}\,{\rm erg\,s^{-1}}$ , and AGN radio/jet power (roughly the same) – they are powered by the same lepton source.

These are shown in a population and demographics sense in Hopkins et al. (2026b). In Paper I and Hopkins et al. (2025c) we consider Perseus, and argue the same can explain the difference between the apparent SCC with $\dot{M}_{X}\sim 1000\,{\rm M_{\odot}\,yr^{-1}}$ and a “true” underlying WCC with $\dot{M}_{\rm true}\sim 10\,{\rm M_{\odot}\,yr^{-1}}$ . Here, the apparent WCC could have an even much weaker “true” WCC with $\dot{M}_{\rm true}\lesssim 0.1\,{\rm M_{\rm odot}\,yr^{-1}}$ , but is also consistent with effectively no CC whatsoever in the underlying gas. This is outside $>1\,$ kpc – at smaller radii well within the ISM (not the CGM/halo) there is a small amount of gas and very small amount of star formation observed (§ 1), powering M87∗’s accretion, but the stellar wind mass loss rate in the central sub-kpc region of M87 is expected to be $\sim 0.1\,{\rm M_{\odot}\,yr^{-1}}$ , more than sufficient to power this, and there is no need (nor is there any evidence) for this to be connected to the extended ICM/CGM/halo.

#### 3.2.2 Central Metallicity Suppression

As discussed in Hopkins et al. (2025b); Hopkins et al. (2026b), this also can explain the apparent metallicity suppression in the Virgo center. Almost all single-temperature X-ray fits to M87 (Böhringer et al., 2001; Molendi and Gastaldello, 2001; Matsushita et al., 2002; Churazov et al., 2008; Russell et al., 2015) have found that the central $Z_{X}$ fit to the X-ray spectrum either rises more slowly compared to the UV/optical metallicity or even stops rising and turns over, decreasing towards $R\rightarrow 0$ . Similar results are found in most well-resolved CCs (almost all with the central $\lesssim 10\,$ kpc resolved; see Matsushita et al. 2002; Rasmussen and Ponman 2007; Komiyama et al. 2009; Million et al. 2010; Murakami et al. 2011; Walker et al. 2013; Panagoulia et al. 2015; Sanders et al. 2016; Gatuzz et al. 2023a; Gatuzz et al. 2023b), including e.g. Virgo, Centaurus, Ophiuchus, NGC 383/2300/4325/5044/6338, HGC 42/62, Abell 262/1991/3581, and others. Matsushita et al. (2002) conducted a survey of systematics in M87 with XMM. They showed that the effect is weaker if one fits only the Fe-K line region in Virgo ( $\gtrsim 4\,$ keV; consistent with the recent spatially un-resolved XRISM spectra, XRISM Collaboration et al. 2025), as compared to the overall spectral shape of the X-rays ( $0.5-8$ keV) or just the Fe-L complex ( $\sim 1\,$ keV). Similarly they found a weaker effect fitting a two-temperature model (which allows a different spectral shape and Fe-L complex behavior from Fe-K). Molendi and Gastaldello (2001) attempted to marginalize away the $Z$ -drop and found this demanded adding a range of additional temperature components and an explicit non-thermal component contaminating the lower-energy X-rays (and their X-ray best-fit still featured highly sub-solar O and Mg with $Z_{\rm O,\,Mg}\sim 0.15-0.4\,Z_{\odot}$ ). Similar results were found by Russell et al. (2018), who still found a central drop (by a factor $\sim 4$ in $Z$ ) even after fitting a three-temperature (with effective temperatures $\sim 0.1-3\,$ keV) plus explicit non-thermal AGN/nuclear spectrum model.

These suggest that something has suppressed the equivalent width of metal lines in the central regions of Virgo, at lower energies $\sim$ keV in particular. But even the Fe-K or two-temperature $Z_{X}$ appears suppressed relative to UV/optical diagnostics of the metallicity in Virgo at $\lesssim 10\,$ kpc, which we compile from stellar metallicity measurements (each using different tracers and different instruments for their measurements) in Davies et al. (1993); Liu et al. (2005); Kuntschner et al. (2010); Montes et al. (2014). Note that much of the systematic offset between some of these measurements can be attributed to those which are sensitive to $\alpha$ abundances (e.g. Davies et al. 1993) versus Fe (Liu et al., 2005), with [ $\alpha$ /Fe] $\sim 0.3-0.4$ in M87 as in most massive ellipticals. We also show the gas-phase ISM metallicity measurements (of $Z$ and Fe), including the $95\%$ range observed, for BCGs of the same stellar mass as Virgo (Gu et al. 2022; Zhuang et al. 2024), and the recently-measured gas metallicity values directly in M87 itself from MUSE/VLT observations of high-resolution emission-line spectroscopy in optical/UV wavelengths (Olivares et al., 2025). Note the latter include the effect of several different line calibration choices and template ionization spectra as part of their quoted error budget. This discrepancy between X-ray and optical/UV determined metallicities, for gas at the same radius in the same galaxy, follows what is predicted for CR-IC in the models here.

As discussed in Hopkins et al. (2026b) and Paper I, the central $Z_{X}$ predicted here is a very crude estimate, based on a simple ratio of the continuum emission around Fe-L and Fe-K (a proxy for the equivalent-width suppression of the lines). We do not model spectral fitting in detail, as it is well-known that $Z_{X}$ is quite sensitive to instrumental properties, fitting procedures, energy range, temperature model priors, and other choices (Matsushita et al., 2002; Mazzotta et al., 2004; Ghizzardi et al., 2021; ZuHone et al., 2023), and we neglect (likely weaker) CR line excitation effects. Despite these simplifications, the predicted $Z_{X}$ is still quite sensitive to what we assume for the underlying thermal emission, as the lines are highly temperature-sensitive. This is obvious in Fig. 2, and shown for a wider range of models in Paper I, as well as models in Hopkins et al. (2026b) which allow for a more realistic distribution of temperatures. What is important is that (a) all models with strong CR-IC produce some central metallicity suppression relative to UV/optical, as observed, and (b) different detailed assumptions for the background gas and fitting assumptions applied to the combined spectrum can reproduce the range of observed $Z_{X}$ trends, including the more extreme central drops seen in some $Z_{X}$ estimates.

#### 3.2.3 On Central Temperatures

Briefly we note that in Fig. 2, we assume (for simplicity) that the true temperature $T_{\rm true}$ remains flat as $R\rightarrow 0$ . Thus the suppression of the central $T_{X}$ owes to CR-IC at low X-ray energies. However, we stress that this is not necessary or important for the model. It is perfectly possible that the true temperature $T_{\rm true}$ does decrease in the Virgo center, especially if the CR-IC scenario is true, since the prediction of the model (Fig. 2) is that the central pressure becomes CR dominated at $R\lesssim 10-20\,$ kpc, and it is very well-established that CR-pressure-dominated halos support and stabilize cooler CGM/ICM gas (Ji et al., 2020; Hopkins et al., 2021a; Ji et al., 2021; Hopkins et al., 2021b; Butsky et al., 2020; Weber et al., 2025), governed globally by buoyant dynamics (Hopkins et al., 2021a). If that were the case, then the (already small) bias of $T_{X}$ from CR-IC would be even smaller, and if we modeled a somewhat harder CR spectrum it could even slightly bias the temperature higher. But importantly in any case the temperature bias from CR-IC is quite weak, or even non-existant. The important effect of CR-IC is boosting the SB/luminosity and therefore X-ray apparent density $n_{X}$ , which is what drives all of the other effects discussed above.

### 3.3 Radio

Fig. 3 shows the corresponding radio properties in the models here. We compile published, reduced maps of the diffuse radio surface brightness from $\sim$ few to $\sim 40-100\,$ kpc scales from: 144 MHz LOFAR (Edler et al., 2023); 325 MHz VLA (Owen et al., 2000); 99, 130, 166, 196, 227 MHz MWA and 1063, 1711, 2563 MHz VLA (Wu et al., 2025); 25, 36, 48, 59, 71, 140 MHz LOFAR LBA and 1400, 1600 MHz VLA (de Gasperin et al., 2012); 54, 144 MHz LOFAR plus 1284 MHz MEERKAT (de Gasperin et al., 2025); 900, 1000, 1120, 1230, 1340, 1440, 1550, 1660 MHz MEERKAT (Mtshweni, 2022); and 10550 MHz Effelsberg (Rottmann et al., 1996). From each, we can construct the spectrum and intensity $S_{\nu}$ in azimuthal annuli $R$ , between radii from a few times the central beamsize (as defined by the authors) to an outer radius which we take to be that where the majority of pixels are above the detection limit quoted for each map. Importantly, we do not simply compare a linear average of the intensity in each annulus, but show the median and $\sim 90\%$ inclusion interval of the range of intensities within the annulus. Cursory examination of the maps reflects the well-known fact that at some radii, especially at higher frequencies, the mean is completely dominated by small (non-volume-filling) bright regions or hot spots (these typically correspond to the jet edges/shocks and radio “ear” features), while we are interested in and only model the diffuse volume-filling (lower-intensity) gas emission.

We see the simple models here reasonably reproduce the radial profiles in both normalization and shape, at frequencies from $\sim 20\,$ MHz to $\sim 1.5$ GHz. The detailed shape does differ, with the observations showing a sort of flat “shelf” behavior at $\sim 8-20\,$ kpc, but this is well known and related to the extended jets/injection region (which we cannot capture in the models here, as we approximate the injection as point-like for simplicity). More important though is (1) the profiles are cut off by losses at roughly the correct radii; (2) their relative amplitudes are consistent, indicating that the radio spectrum is plausible and steepens with $R$ akin to the observations as CRs age; and (3) the normalization is plausible. In short, the same CR lepton density profiles which reproduce the X-ray properties are consistent with the radio properties out to tens of kpc. We also plot more detailed spectra of the predicted diffuse radio from $\sim 1-10^{4}\,$ MHz. These show the same, and demonstrate more clearly the un-ambiguous spectral hardening with increasing $R$ observed and discussed extensively in a number of radio studies (de Gasperin et al., 2012; Mtshweni, 2022; Wu et al., 2025). This suggests a population of aging leptons streaming from the central source, constraining both their power and effective streaming speed to be something like that adopted here. Indeed, the combination of the soft X-ray, radio, and Faraday rotation (§ 3.5.1) makes it challenging to construct models where CR-IC is negligible for X-rays in the core ( $\lesssim 10-20\,$ kpc).

While we assume a simple, spherically-symmetric model so cannot model X-ray or radio fluctuations in the 2D maps (or turbulence/shocks/etc.), these should of course be present. Several of the studies above (see e.g. de Gasperin et al. 2012; de Gasperin et al. 2025; Edler et al. 2023, but also Forman et al. 2007 who approach the same from the X-ray side comparing to Owen et al. 2000) have shown that in the diffuse gas, like in most CC clusters at low frequencies (outside of the active jet/cocoon structure; see Giacintucci et al. 2011; Giacintucci et al. 2019; Bravi et al. 2016; Balboni et al. 2024; Riseley et al. 2023; Riseley et al. 2024), there is an unambiguous positive correlation between soft X-ray and low-frequency radio surface brightness, both globally (radial profiles) and at fixed radius (azimuthally). This is of course trivially expected in a CR-IC model (with scatter and systemic variations coming from CR acceleration/injection and $B$ -field variations).

### 3.4 Other Wavelengths: UVOIR, Hard X-rays, & Gamma-Rays

Fig. 4 shows the predicted spectra from CR emission at $10^{10}\,$ Hz (3 cm) through $10^{16}\,$ Hz (41 eV or 300 Å). As expected, the direct CR emission is orders-of-magnitude below the metagalactic backgrounds (Cooray, 2016; Khaire and Srianand, 2019) and stellar+dust+gas emission spectra at these wavelengths (compiled from NED averaged within an effective aperture of $10\,$ kpc, with the ICL SED specifically coming from the differential/narrow annular regions at $10$ and $100\,$ kpc, using the bands and colors available from Kormendy et al. 2009; Rudick et al. 2010; Krick et al. 2011 spanning $4.5\,{\rm\mu m}$ to $U$ -band). We also denote in the EUV where Galactic absorption severely limits any constraints, for the standard Galactic column $\sim 4-5\times 10^{20}\,{\rm cm^{-2}}$ in the direction of the Virgo core.

More interesting, Fig. 4 also shows the harder X-rays up to $\sim 400\,$ keV. At energies $\gtrsim 10\,$ keV, detection of the emission around M87 is challenging, as (1) the relatively low luminosity and extended size on the sky make it comparable to the metagalactic background and often well below the instrument background of hard X-ray detectors like NuSTAR or Switft-BAT, and (2) there is a nearby Seyfert galaxy nucleus NGC 4388 which is extremely bright at these energies, so must be separated (but this is especially difficult given typical angular resolution at these energies). Nonetheless, with higher resolution, NuSTAR has a robust detection within a $\sim 30^{\prime\prime}$ ( $<2.4\,$ kpc) radius aperture at both $20-40$ and $10-40$ keV (Wong et al., 2017; Imazawa et al., 2021), where we take the flux range to be the baseline where they detect no evidence for spatial or time variation over baselines as long as years, indicating this comes from extended diffuse gas or jets (and not the AGN nucleus). Abdo et al. (2009) attempt to place an upper limit on emission within a few kpc from Swift-BAT, which we include but stress is highly-sensitive to the assumed instrument background subtraction and NGC4388 separation (likely explaining its apparent tension with the subsequent higher-resolution NuSTAR detections). Walter (2009) detect M87 well above-background with robust separation from NGC 4388, in what appears to be extended emission from $\sim 10-30\,$ kpc at $20-60\,$ keV. de Jong et al. (2015) argue that with different background models and multi-year time-averaging this INTEGRAL detection decreases in magnitude but they instead detect extended (time-steady/non-varying) emission from a larger $\sim 100\,$ kpc aperture with Suzaku HXD. We show all of these, for completeness. Note we include $\sim 0.1-10\,$ keV emission in our soft X-ray profiles (Fig. 2), but show it here as well for a couple radii as a useful anchor point, since this is much better measured with instruments like Chandra and ASCA (Allen et al., 2000, we specifically show the X-ray spectra directly measured to $10\,$ keV in at a matched $\sim 30\,$ kpc aperture in). In any case we see the models are consistent with all of these. Outside the M87 injection region ( $\gtrsim 10\,$ kpc) they generally predict thermal-like spectra consistent with the soft X-rays which fall off rapidly to $\sim 20\,$ keV, with some low-level flux (below the metagalactic background) from CR-IC of higher-energy (infrared-optical) seed photons.

The diffuse $\gamma$ -ray flux is dominated by relativistic bremsstrahlung at $\sim 100\,$ MeV. However, Fig. 4 shows this is quite weak: the extended emission is below the metagalactic background, significantly below (especially at $\gtrsim$ GeV energies) the detected $\gamma$ -rays from M87∗ and its jets (compiled from Abdo et al. 2009; H. E. S. S. Collaboration et al. 2024; Ait Benkhali et al. 2019) from Fermi, HESS, MAGIC, and VERITAS, and orders-of-magnitude below the best present upper limits on diffuse $\gamma$ -ray emission from Fermi (constraint shown from Ackermann et al. 2015, but see also Han et al. 2012 who obtain very similar upper limits). Because the cutoff is extremely steep, there is basically no predicted emission at TeV for any higher-energy instrument. If we introduced a population of CR hadrons with comparable escaping energy to the leptons at $\gtrsim 1\,$ kpc, like in Paper I, this would introduce a second bump from pionic interactions of comparable flux, at $\sim 1-10\,$ GeV, with a shallower power-law tail, but it would still be below the central detection. Thus hadron-to-lepton total energy ratios as large as $\sim 30$ (larger than observed in the LISM, once accounting for the integral over the entire energy range; see Bisschoff et al. 2019) could be accommodated in the diffuse gas in Virgo without violating $\gamma$ -ray constraints. Of course, if there were such a large hadron population, the total CR acceleration rate of M87 would need to be correspondingly higher, and the CR pressure would be correspondingly larger (so Virgo would be CR-pressure dominated out to a larger radius). Like with Perseus, another allowed scenario is that the leptons invoked here are primarily produced via pionic interactions of hadrons on small scales (i.e. the acceleration is hadronic, but those convert an order-one fraction of their energy to leptons before escaping to $\gg$ kpc scales). We are agnostic to all of these because it is really the leptons which influence all the other observables we consider.22 2 Note that the models here clearly are well below the $\gamma$ -ray upper limits, despite CR pressure dominating the total pressure budget interior to $\lesssim 10-20\,$ kpc. H. E. S. S. Collaboration et al. (2023) claimed that the total $\gamma$ -ray flux from Virgo sets an upper limit of a few percent of the pressure from CRs, but their constraint (1) applies to an average over much larger radii (does not constrain the CR pressure in the Virgo center); (2) assumes all the CRs are hadronic with negligible leptons; (3) assumes an order-of-magnitude higher gas density $n_{X}$ so is order-of-magnitude weaker when correcting for the CR-IC corrected true gas density in Fig. 2; and (4) assumes an extremely hard, pure-power-law CR spectrum, so a large fraction of the CR energy is at energies $\gtrsim$ TeV, completely unlike the spectra we model. As such there is no tension between even $10-30\,$ times larger CR pressure than we predict, and the $\gamma$ -ray observations.

### 3.5 Independent Constraints

Fig. 5 compares various additional, indirect model constraints, on magnetic field strengths, mass/potential profiles, and the Sunyaev-Zeldovich (SZ) effect.

#### 3.5.1 Magnetic Fields & Tension Intrinsic to the “Pure Thermal X-rays” Model

There are rich measurements of Faraday rotation measures (RMs) towards the center of M87, from the compact radio core on scales $\lesssim$ pc down to near-horizon (au) scales (Matveyenko and Seleznev, 2014; Kuo et al., 2014; Li et al., 2016; Avachat et al., 2016; Algaba et al., 2016; Pasetto et al., 2021; Tsunetoe et al., 2022; Peng et al., 2024). As the number and quality of RM measurements have increased, a very robust result is that the RMs vary dramatically on small angular/spatial ( $\lesssim$ pc) and time ( $\lesssim$ yr) scales, which places very strong upper limits on the RM contribution from the diffuse ICM with fields on $\gtrsim$ kpc coherence scales. Park et al. (2019) consider a large ensemble of these and argue this is approximately $|{\rm RM}_{\rm ICM}|\lesssim 130\,{\rm rad\,m^{-2}}$ , with about a factor of $<2$ uncertainty. This is consistent with Algaba et al. 2016; Tsunetoe et al. 2022; Peng et al. 2024, who all place upper limits $\ll 1000\,{\rm rad\,m^{-2}}$ from the ICM, and consistent with the qualitative conclusions of the other RM studies above that all argue the RMs must come from within or very close to the inner accretion disk/jet core, jets, or jet sheaths. Given ${\rm RM}=812\,{\rm rad\,m^{-2}}\,\int_{0}^{\infty}(n_{e}/{\rm cm^{-3}})\,(B_{\|}/{\rm\mu G})\,(d\ell/{\rm kpc})$ , this implies an upper limit (assuming isotropic fields) of $|{\bf B}|\lesssim B_{\rm max}\sim 0.28\,{\rm\mu G}/\int_{0}^{\infty}n_{e}d\ell/({\rm cm^{-3}kpc})$ . For a given model of $n_{e}(r)$ , we therefore immediately obtain the corresponding $B_{\rm max}$ , shown in Fig. 5. We plot this first for the default model here, where $n_{e}$ is relatively low and the X-rays come primarily from CR-IC, and show it is compatible with the magnetic field profile we assume. Note that we specifically adopt a model $B(r)$ near the high-end allowed, because any weaker field means that it is even more likely that for the given observed radio emission, the X-rays should primarily come from CR-IC, so this is the “worst-case scenario” for the CR-IC models here. But we also show $B_{\rm max}(r)$ in the traditional interpretation of the soft X-rays as thermal emission: because producing the observed SB with just thermal emission requires much larger densities $n_{e}$ at a given $r$ , the RM upper limit then requires $B_{\rm max}$ is much lower, $\ll{\rm\mu G}$ at essentially all radii even in the M87 ISM, which seems unphysical.

Note that we can also estimate an upper limit on $B$ from kinematics, arguing that there cannot be more than a certain fraction of additional pressure or it would unbind the cluster. We have computed this, but these constraints are significantly weaker than the RM constraints shown.

We can also place a lower limit on $B$ , $|{\bf B}|\gtrsim B_{\rm min}$ , from the combination of radio profiles and hard X-ray emission. This is a standard technique (Cova et al., 2019; Creech et al., 2024, e.g.), and uses the fact that CR leptons which radiate at a synchrotron frequency $\sim 10\,{\rm MHz}\,B_{\rm\mu G}\,E_{\rm GeV}^{2}$ will also produce CR-IC from the CMB at X-ray energy $\sim 3\,{\rm keV}\,E_{\rm GeV}^{2}$ , with a ratio of specific emissivity $\propto e_{\rm cmb}/e_{\rm B}$ . Given the ranges allowed, the most powerful constraint comes from combining the 20 MHz radio profile with the $\sim 20-60\,$ keV X-ray emission (for which we take the highest values in Fig. 4, as any lower value would lead to an even-larger upper limit in $B_{\rm min}$ , so this is the most conservative possible choice). We plot this over the range where there is some constraint on the integrated flux in both bands. We can also estimate the same by combining the GHz radio with GeV $\gamma$ ray emission (shown), but this is somewhat less constraining. In either case this sets lower limits around $\sim 0.2-0.3\,{\rm\mu G}$ .

We immediately see that there is some tension, purely empirically, between the “thermal-only” assumption for soft X-rays coupled to the observed RMs and the observed radio and hard X-ray upper limits. This is not yet at a level that we can say the thermal-only soft X-ray models are conclusively ruled out from Fig. 5 alone, but the tension is noteworthy.
