#### 3.5.2 Mass Models and Evidence for Non-Thermal Components

Fig. 5 shows the 3D mass profile $M(<r)$ of Virgo, from different reconstruction methods. We compile several non-X-ray studies using stellar plus globular cluster kinematics (Murphy et al., 2011; Liepold et al., 2023), satellite kinematics (Kashibadze et al., 2020), and SZ (Planck Collaboration et al., 2016). In the latter, the SZ is not used for a pressure profile, but rather, to infer the baryonic mass on the assumption of the X-ray fitted temperature (at large radii) being correct, then assuming a universal baryon fraction. We compare several X-ray studies assuming hydrostatic equilibrium (Matsushita et al., 2002; Churazov et al., 2008; Das et al., 2010; Simionescu et al., 2017), and our own reconstruction using the de-projected X-ray profiles in Urban et al. (2011). We compare the fiducial adopted mass model ( $M_{\rm vir}=6\times 10^{14}\,{\rm M_{\odot}}$ , $M_{200c}\approx 5\times 10^{14}\,{\rm M_{\odot}}$ ) and a “light” halo $M_{\rm vir}=1.5\times 10^{14}\,{\rm M_{\odot}}$ ( $M_{200c}\approx 1.2\times 10^{14}\,{\rm M_{\odot}}$ ). Recall, the CR-IC+thermal emission models here reproduce the observed X-ray profiles in their “apparent” X-ray emission, so the inferred mass profile from them will necessarily be the same as the observations plotted.

A few interesting points emerge. The X-ray and kinematic data differ significantly at many radii, contrary to earlier claims in e.g. Churazov et al. (2008) which featured much larger systematic uncertainties in both kinematic models (e.g. their reference Wu and Tremaine 2006, which quoted factor $\sim 6$ uncertainties at the salient radii) and X-ray data (the large radial fluctuations in Fig. 5 in the Churazov et al. 2008 data). Most notably, at small radii $\lesssim 20\,$ kpc, the updated X-ray data and hydrostatic masses with much smaller error bars from the same authors in Das et al. (2010) (also Matsushita et al. 2002) appear to under-estimate the enclosed mass by factors of several (while Churazov et al. 2008 oscillates by factors of several around $M(<r)$ ), when compared to the newer kinematic constraints (e.g. Murphy et al. 2011; Agnello et al. 2014; Liepold et al. 2023), that leverage newer, higher-resolution resolved HST+IFU spectroscopy, expanded globular kinematics, gas kinematics, and more sophisticated triaxial jeans modeling with expanded black hole+stellar+dark matter models. At large radii $\gtrsim 50\,$ kpc the same factor-of-few oscillations are evident, and the X-ray data appears to systematically favor a surprisingly low total mass of $\sim 1\times 10^{14}\,{\rm M_{\odot}}$ (Urban et al., 2011; Simionescu et al., 2017), in apparent contradiction to constraints from (1) SZ (Planck Collaboration et al., 2016), (2) satellite kinematics (Kashibadze et al., 2020), and (3) large-scale infall motions of filaments and galaxies outside of the Virgo virial radius (Lee et al., 2015), all of which appear to favor a virial mass $\sim 5-8\times 10^{14}\,M_{\odot}$ .33 3 Also, regardless of the “light” or “heavy” halo, both require somewhat high values of the concentration parameter $c_{\rm vir}\equiv R_{\rm vir}/R_{s,\,{\rm NFW}}$ , specifically $c_{\rm vir}\sim 7.5$ for the “heavy” halo and $c_{\rm vir}\sim 10$ for the “light” halo ( $c_{200c}\sim 5.6,\,7.5$ , respectively), to match the observations at $\sim 40-150\,$ kpc – about a $+2\sigma$ deviation from the standard $c-M$ relation (Merten et al., 2015; Biviano et al., 2017). We stress that this has no effect on our modeling in this paper, as it only becomes important ourside $\gtrsim 200-300\,$ kpc where CR-IC is negligible, and CRs cannot plausibly explain the discrepancy, but it suggests (as noted in several of the papers above) that either some of the observations are incorrect or that there is substantial non-equilibrium (and/or non-hydrostatic, or non-spherical) structure in Virgo at $\gtrsim 0.2-0.3\,R_{500}$ . There are many possibilities. The discrepancy at smaller radii is more interesting for the models here. Note that even where the X-ray and kinematics appear to agree well (e.g. $\sim 15-40\,$ kpc), the rms deviations between the two are $\sim 20-50\%$ , comparable to the systematic uncertainties in both (just measuring the X-ray profile along different azimuthal angles, or using slightly different tracer populations for the stellar kinematics, give different results at this level). And at small radii $\lesssim 10\,$ kpc, where the kinematic constraints are best, there is a much larger factor-of-few discrepancy, and this has been shown and discussed in many previous studies as the kinematic data have improved (and similar discrepancies have been noted for the locally-peaked X-ray profiles around other, individual galaxies within Virgo, e.g. Shen and Gebhardt 2010 and references therein). This makes it easy, for example, to accommodate a predominant CR pressure, buoyant motions in the ICM, and non-equilibrium effects.

#### 3.5.3 The Sunyaev-Zeldovich Effect: Less Sensitive in Weak Cool Cores

Fig. 5 also shows the predicted ratio of SZ-inferred pressure $P_{\rm SZ}$ to X-ray inferred pressure $P_{X}$ , on the assumption that the observed “apparent” X-ray pressure (Fig. 2) is interpreted as thermal, together with the same ratio from Planck observations in the outer ICM (Planck Collaboration et al., 2016). As described in Hopkins et al. (2025b), because of CR-IC boosting $n_{X}$ , the X-ray pressure $P_{X}$ is over-estimated in the central regions so $P_{\rm SZ}/P_{X}$ is suppressed, but this is a mild effect for a weak CC like Virgo, compared to SCCs discussed therein and in Paper I. We see that the predictions are completely compatible with present SZ constraints, but these are only at very large radii. Given Virgo’s large size on the sky, potential contamination by the jets at $R\lesssim 10\,$ kpc, and the relatively small magnitude of the predicted effect, it is unlikely the predicted difference will be robustly observed with present instruments.

## 4 Differences from SCCs like Perseus?

Here we briefly comment on the major differences between plausible models like those here for CR-IC in a WCC like Virgo, versus CR-IC models like those in Paper I for SCCs like Perseus. First, per § 3.2.1, a key physical interpretation difference is that in SCCs like Perseus, the CR-IC models still favor (and probably require) some cooling and multi-phase gas in the ICM, just 100 $\times$ less than the naive classical SCC cooling-flow problem would imply. Thus an “apparent” SCC can become a “true” WCC. Starting from an apparent WCC like Virgo, where there is no evidence for cooling gas at $\gtrsim$ kpc scales, the apparent WCC can become a “true” NCC.

Of course, some properties are different in the models for Virgo, but in a way that is not interesting for the physics we explore: the CR injection rate $\dot{E}_{\rm cr}$ is $\sim 100$ times lower in our Virgo model compared to Perseus, but this simply reflects the observed difference in the radio+ $\gamma$ -ray+X-ray luminosities of the clusters. And of course the large-radii/“underlying” gas density/temperature/metallicity profiles differ but just as expected for different mass clusters (as the cluster masses differ by an order of magnitude).

### 4.1 Softer Injection Spectra

Turning to non-trivial differences relevant for the actual physics here, first we note that comparing to Paper I and Perseus, the nominally favored CR-IC models here have somewhat softer effective CR injection (emergent from $\sim$ kpc) spectra. As discussed in § 3.2.3, some of this is driven by our arbitrary assumption that the “true” temperature $T$ is constant at small radii, so the apparent lower $T_{X}\sim 1\,$ keV must be driven by CRs, which therefore requires a soft CR spectrum at small radii. But as emphasized there, this is not necessary – especially in CR-pressure dominated central regions, the physical temperatures could and perhaps should be cooler, so (because the effect of CR-IC on the inferred $T_{X}$ is relatively weak), modeling that would allow for significantly harder injection spectra. However there is still a clear indication of softer injection spectra from both radio and hard X-ray observations: while Perseus is clearly detected by NuStar, Hitomi, Swift-BAT, Integral, and many others with a very significant hard X-ray component, per § 3.4 that is weaker in Virgo. More clearly, the radio spectral index in the central regions is significantly softer in Virgo: in the central ( $\sim$ kpc, here, not the radio core on sub-pc scales) regions from LOFAR observations and other low-frequency ( $\lesssim 150\,$ MHz) data, the spectral index never gets much shallower than $\alpha\sim 0.6$ or so (outside of very specific “hot spots” like the jet shocks/lobes/“ears”), while for the central regions of NGC 1275/3C 84 (the Perseus BCG) this index approaches more like $\alpha\sim 0$ . So this is not a difference unique to the CR-IC interpretation, but a purely empirical question.

In terms of explanations, it is plausible to understand if, for example, the acceleration region in the M87 core is more compact (compared to the more extended jets/lobes/cocoons/shocks around NGC 1275), and contained within the dense gas, strong magnetic field, and strong radiation energy-density region on sub-kpc scales around M87∗. The emergent spectrum at $\gtrsim$ kpc could therefore plausibly be more significantly influenced by losses “on the way out.” But there are many other possibilities as well.

### 4.2 Transport Parameters

Looking at the CR transport parameters $\kappa$ (effective isotropic diffusivity) and $v_{\rm st}$ (effective bulk streaming speed, including advection/super and Alfvénic streaming, super-diffusion, or radially-dependent diffusion), although the value of the total “effective transport speed” $v_{\rm eff}\sim v_{\rm st}+\kappa/r$ is broadly similar to that in Paper I from $\sim 10-100\,$ kpc, the fiducial values here involve a lower diffusivity $\kappa$ and higher streaming speed $v_{\rm st}$ , compared to the fiducial Perseus model in Paper I. This preference is driven entirely by the shape of the central radio and X-ray surface brightness profiles in Virgo versus Perseus: Virgo has a much steeper radio/X-ray brightness and therefore inferred-density $n_{X}$ profile at all radii $\lesssim 100\,$ kpc, compared to Perseus (e.g. $\epsilon_{X}\propto n_{X}^{2}\propto r^{-2}$ versus $\propto r^{-1}$ , a difference of a factor of $\sim 100$ in emissivity over this radial range). Given the simplicity of our default models, where the injection is point-like, both $\kappa$ and $v_{\rm st}$ are constant, and the clusters are spherically symmetric and in steady-state, the steady-state emissivity from CR-IC scales $\propto e_{\rm cr}\propto 1/(v_{\rm st}\,r^{2})$ in the streaming-dominated limit ( $v_{\rm st}\gg\kappa/r$ ) or $\propto 1/(\kappa\,r)$ in the diffusion-dominated limit.

This could arise, in principle, from variations in the microphysics of CR scattering and different plasma and/or CR properties (values of $B$ , $n$ , $T$ , strength of turbulence, CR energy density, etc.). What actually sets the microphysical CR scattering rates on $\sim 0.1\,{\rm au}$ scales (the spatial scales relevant for magnetic field fluctuations which scatter CRs of the energy range of interest here), which in turn controls the physical values and scalings of $\kappa$ or $v_{\rm st}$ , is deeply physically uncertain (even in the LISM where CR measurements are most accurate), and as a result different first-principles plasma physics models predict qualitatively different scalings of these parameters that can differ by as much as $\sim 10$ orders-of-magnitude in the CGM/ICM (Hopkins et al., 2021b; Hopkins et al., 2021c; Hopkins et al., 2022b; Ponnada et al., 2024b; Ponnada et al., 2024a; Fitz Axen et al., 2024; Ponnada et al., 2025; Su et al., 2025; Lu et al., 2025). So it is ambiguous to interpret this in terms of any specific CR microphysics.

Alternatively, this effect could be related to other, more resolvable properties. If in Virgo, advection in buoyant modes or winds or the jets themselves is more important, the CR transport could be more “streaming-like” because CRs are simply carried by bulk motions. Alternatively, as noted in § 4.1, this could also relate to the effective spatial scale of injection. The flatter profile in Perseus could arise not because of more-diffusive transport from a point-source-like injection, but rather from the same transport parameters as Virgo, but a more spread-out injection region extending to several tens of kpc (the size of the lobes/cavities). Future modeling in more detailed cluster simulations with CR dynamics can make more robust predictions for these, but in simplified analytic models like those here these different scenarios are largely degenerate.

### 4.3 Lack of a Giant Radio Halo

In Paper I, we showed that the CR-IC models can also produce a giant radio halo extending to $\sim$ Mpc. This does not come from CRs injected by the central source, no matter how luminous, as the leptons cannot reach $\gtrsim$ Mpc scales before losing their energy to IC. But per Hopkins et al. (2025a); Hopkins et al. (2025b), every cluster galaxy, even low-mass (Milky Way-like or smaller) galaxies, produces its own CR “mini-mini-halo”, which appears in IC around isolated Milky Way and M31-mass galaxies in ROSAT and eROSITA soft X-ray survey stacks (Zhang et al., 2024), and is clearly evident in the extended $\gamma$ -ray emission observed in the Milky Way (Acero et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2016; Pothast et al., 2018) and M31 (Abdo et al., 2010; Karwin et al., 2019). Each extends to $\sim 100\,$ kpc, but their individual surface brightness is extremely low (lower than the central-galaxy halo by approximately the ratio of their CR injection rates, and further suppressed by weaker magnetic fields in the cluster outskirts), but because they effectively overlap in projection, they collectively can be observed in a case like Perseus (Paper I). The same process should happen in Virgo, and we in fact calculate this collective contribution in the profiles shown in Fig. 3 using the Virgo projected galaxy number density compiled in Kashibadze et al. (2020) and assuming a total CR injection rate from Virgo satellites a factor of $\sim 0.1$ times the M87 injection rate (the same ratio observed in Perseus, and consistent with the ratio of radio luminosity of the satellites, though that could be as low as $\sim 0.02-0.1$ Capetti et al. 2009; Vollmer et al. 2013; Spasic et al. 2024). But this immediately explains why the predicted giant halo is negligible in Fig. 3: (1) the Virgo injection rate is $\sim 100$ times smaller than Perseus, and (2) Virgo’s extended halo is $\sim 100$ times larger on the sky. This not only makes it infeasible to observe the whole cluster, but means the predicted surface brightness of the giant halo from this source is $\sim 10^{4}$ times fainter. Given that the giant halo in Perseus has only just been detected by new, extremely deep integrations from the most sensitive instruments and wavelengths in LOFAR (van Weeren et al., 2024), it is clear that we do not expect to see the same in Virgo.

## 5 Conclusions

We show that a simple model of CR leptons injected in M87∗ with a kinetic luminosity comparable to the usual value inferred from the compact radio and $\gamma$ -ray spectra/variability, and propagating outwards in Virgo in steady-state with a streaming speed $\sim 100\,{\rm km\,s^{-1}}$ (subject to standard losses), can naturally explain a wide variety of observations from radio ( $\sim 10^{6}-10^{11}\,$ Hz) and soft X-rays ( $\sim 0.1-10\,$ keV), without contradicting any limits from harder X-ray or $\gamma$ -rays, SZ, Faraday rotation, or dynamical/mass/potential reconstruction constraints, at radii $\sim 1-1000\,$ kpc. These models predict that the central, steeply-rising soft X-ray surface brightness interior to $\lesssim 20\,$ kpc has a significant contribution from thermal-continuum-like (highly curved/non-power-law) inverse-Compton scattered CMB photons.

This naturally explains the “cooling flow problem” in M87: the true cooling rate in the model is much lower ( $\sim 0.1\,{\rm M_{\odot}\,yr^{-1}}$ ) than the cooling rate inferred if one assumes the X-rays are purely thermal ( $\sim 10\,{\rm M_{\odot}\,yr^{-1}}$ ). It simultaneously explains the shape of the central CC soft X-ray profiles in surface brightness $S_{X}$ , inferred thermodynamic properties ( $n_{X}$ , $T_{X}$ , $P_{X}$ , $K_{X}$ , $\dot{M}_{X}$ ), and metallicity $Z_{X}$ (explaining the apparent metallicity suppression inferred in $\sim$ keV X-rays but not optical/UV or harder/Fe-K X-rays in $Z$ within a few kpc), as well as the apparent tight correlation between the M87 jet/radio power and X-ray cooling luminosity (both powered by the same lepton source). It also explains the radio spectrum and surface brightness profiles of the diffuse, ultra-steep volume-filling radio halo of M87 on these scales, and its clear spectral curvature and steepening with distance from M87∗.

We further show that new Faraday rotation measure (RM) limits on the magnetic field strongly argue for a significant CR-IC contribution at small radii, as otherwise (with the much larger gas densities required to reproduce the soft X-rays in a thermal-only scenario) the RM upper limits to $B$ in the diffuse cluster gas at $\lesssim 30\,$ kpc would be unphysically low ( $\lesssim 0.1\,{\rm\mu G}$ ), and in tension with lower limits on $B$ from the combination of the radio detections and hard X-ray emission upper limits.

Together, this suggests that at least some apparent “weak cool core” (WCC) clusters with central radio galaxies, of which Virgo is often considered prototypical, may in fact have true thermodynamic properties more consistent with a relaxed-but-not significantly cooling cluster (at least outside $\gtrsim 1\,$ kpc), plus central CR-IC emission. Even more robustly, these indicate that at $\lesssim 10$ kpc around M87, CR pressure must be a significant (and likely dominant, at $\lesssim 5\,$ kpc) fraction of the total pressure in the diffuse gas.

Our model does not explain every feature of Virgo in radio and X-rays, of course. For example, we assume for simplicity spherical symmetry with point-like central CR injection, but it is clear that CRs are also being accelerated or re-accelerated in some special extended jet termination/shock/“radio ear” regions related to the extended jets out to few-kpc scales, which are specifically associated with the regions where higher-frequency synchrotron and less-curved radio spectra are observed. Future work using full dynamical CR-MHD simulations, with injection and transport parameters motivated by the simple analytic models here, would be particularly informative. Interestingly, compared to more extreme radio+X-ray sources like Perseus, we do not predict a detectable giant radio halo (owing to the weaker overall lepton injection and much lower satellite radio source density on the sky), and the radio data imply a softer CR spectrum escaping or accelerated outside of the central $\sim$ kpc, with a somewhat more “streaming-like” (or super-diffusive, or $\kappa\propto R$ ) profile (directly related to the steeper central surface brightness in radio and X-rays observed in Virgo versus Perseus). We discuss a variety of physics that could give rise to these more subtle differences, but given the orders-of-magnitude uncertainty in how CR transport physics scales with ICM/plasma properties, it is difficult to tie these to specific physical models.

Paper I reviewed future observational tests of the picture here. Future spatial-and-spectrally-resolved (de-projected) X-ray spectra at $\sim 1\,$ keV to measure $Z_{X}$ within the CC ( $\lesssim 10\,$ kpc) combined with independent optical/UV gas-phase metallicities $Z_{\rm true}$ constrain CR-IC. Optical data already exists at small- $R$ but future X-ray missions like ATHENA could greatly improve the X-ray side. In radio, mapping diffuse synchrotron (in the CC but outside the jets) at $\lesssim 20\,$ MHz will further improve the overlap of the energy range where leptons emitting in soft X-rays via CR-IC would also emit synchrotron, to test if their implied spectral shapes and emissivities are consistent with the models here (or if, for example, a significant CR-IC emission in X-rays is avoided by the presence of a sudden, very steep cutoff in the radio spectrum just below $\sim 20-40\,$ MHz). Per above, constraints on Faraday rotation in M87 are already powerful, but future independent measurements from background fast radio bursts with impact parameters $\lesssim 10\,$ kpc can rule out pure-thermal emission in X-rays (given the observed radio spectrum) by placing RM upper limits below several thousand ${\rm rad\,m^{-2}}$ . Higher-resolution Sunyaev-Zeldovich observations probing $\ll 20\,$ kpc would be extremely powerful as a constraint on the true thermal pressure, though the “pressure deficit” (ratio $P_{\rm SZ}/P_{\rm X}$ ) is small at most radii outside $\sim 1\,$ kpc as shown above, and these are possible in principle (it requires combining instruments to capture large modes on the sky with high-resolution in the center, but the M87 core has a surface brightness at $\sim 140\,$ GHz nearly $\sim 1000$ times smaller than NGC 1275 in Perseus, and is larger on the sky, so contamination is much less an issue). Strong $\gamma$ -ray constraints require sub-arcminute resolution and at least $\sim 100$ times improved background control (diffuse surface-brightness sensitivity) relative to instruments like Fermi, but this would be powerful at $\sim 10-1000$ MeV energies. Constraints from ionization of dense cold phases in the ICM as available in Perseus can directly measure the number density of low-energy CRs, but are only possible if a significant mass of dense atomic/molecular gas exists embedded within the Virgo ICM at $\sim 10\,$ kpc; thus far searches have only produced upper limits at these radii.

# The Galactic Center $\gamma$ -ray Excess and the Look-Elsewhere Effect

**Authors:** Isabel S. Sands Affiliation: Kavli Institute for Astrophysics and Space Research, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, MA, 02139, USA Philip F. Hopkins Affiliation: TAPIR, California Institute of Technology, Mailcode 350-17, Pasadena, CA 91125, USA

## Abstract

The origin of the excess of GeV $\gamma$ -rays in the Milky Way’s galactic center observed by Fermi-LAT has been an open question for nearly two decades. The two leading interpretations of this signal are that it is produced either by annihilating dark matter (DM), or arises from unresolved point sources, such as a novel population of millisecond pulsars. In both scenarios, uncertainties and limitations in the modeling of galactic diffuse $\gamma$ -ray emission, such as the steady-state approximation of cosmic ray (CR) propagation and assumption of an axisymmetric distribution of CRs, complicate the interpretation of the galactic center excess (GCE). Simulations with full magnetohydrodynamics (MHD) and CR transport can provide a new avenue for understanding the astrophysical phenomena that drive galactic diffuse $\gamma$ -ray emission. We utilize MHD simulations of Milky Way analogs with time-dependent, spectrally-resolved CR transport to reconstruct diffuse $\gamma$ -ray emission. Comparing instantaneous emission to a time-averaged baseline, we find residuals up to several times larger than the Fermi GCE, with a wide range of spectral shapes and spatial morphologies. At some simulation snapshots, the spectrum and morphology of the residuals resemble the Fermi GCE. Our results suggest that the Fermi GCE may be a manifestation of the look-elsewhere effect — a transient fluctuation in diffuse emission from stellar sources, observed at an inopportune moment — and motivate the development of new Fermi-LAT analysis templates that account for time-dependent CR transport.

## I Introduction

Observations from the Fermi Large Area Telescope (LAT) have detected an excess of GeV gamma-rays within the central $\sim 10^{\circ}$ of the Milky Way relative to known astrophysical sources and models of diffuse $\gamma$ -ray emission [14, 15, 1]. More than a decade later, the origin of this signal remains debated, with some literature arguing that the observed excess is a smoking gun for DM annihilation [11, 20, 16], and other studies attributing it to other phenomena such as unresolved point sources (e.g., millisecond pulsars) [23, 4]. Both of these posited explanations have faced challenges: in the case of the annihilating DM hypothesis, some studies have found that the morphology of the excess traces the galactic bulge, indicating an astrophysical origin [24, 5, 34]. However, the morphology of the galactic center (GC) $\gamma$ -ray excess is a matter of ongoing study and debate, with no conclusive answer [22, 21, 27, 31]. The pulsar scenario presents its own set of challenges: the population of progenitor x-ray binaries in the galactic center is not sufficient to produce the number of millisecond pulsars that the $\gamma$ -ray excess requires [13], although the requisite pulsar population could still be generated through more exotic channels [12]. Additionally, recent work has demonstrated that the methods used in some past analyses that favored the pulsar scenario can falsely interpret an injected, spatially-smooth signal consistent with annihilating DM as a collection of point sources [21, 22].

While most of the debate surrounding the GCE has focused on DM and millisecond pulsar origins of the signal, other astrophysical sources have been considered, including non-thermal Bremsstrahlung produced in cosmic ray interactions with molecular clouds near the GC [25, 26], and past activity in the GC from either an AGN or supernovae [30, 24]. However, other studies have suggested that the predominantly leptonic bursts in these scenarios are inconsistent with the uniform spectral shape of the GCE, unless the CR parameters are finely tuned [9, 10]. A major limitation of nearly all past studies of the galactic center excess (GCE) is that they rely on steady-state CR propagation codes that make simplistic assumptions, such as axisymmetric distribution of CRs, and cannot model time-dependent phenomena such as galactic winds, gas coupling to magnetic fields, or turbulence.

Recent numerical developments that enable the simulation of spectrally-resolved CRs in MHD galaxy formation simulations can provide a complementary approach to modeling cosmic ray transport and propagation in galactic environments. It has been demonstrated that CRMHD simulations of Milky Way-like galaxies from cosmological initial conditions can reproduce local interstellar medium (ISM) observations of the CR proton and electron spectra, positron fraction, and $\gamma$ -ray emissivity [17, 32]. In particular, [32] utilized such simulations to model diffuse $\gamma$ -ray emission in the galactic centers of Milky Way-like galaxies from neutral pion ( $\Pi^{0}$ ) decay, non-thermal relativistic Bremsstrahlung, and inverse Compton scattering of CR leptons, finding that the highly dynamical environment drives order-of-magnitude fluctuations in the $\gamma$ -ray spectrum on Myr timescales from supernova-sourced CRs alone.

With the ability to simulate diffuse $\gamma$ -ray emission in full astrophysical context, it is worthwhile to revisit the extent to which CR physics can contribute to the Fermi signal without invoking additional sources. Additionally, simulations allow us to study multiple realizations of Milky Way-mass halos at multiple snapshots in time. In analyzing these simulations, we find that there are transient bumps and wiggles in the GC $\gamma$ -ray spectrum, accompanied by highly-variable morphology of diffuse emission from CR physics. Thus, in this letter, we consider the possibility that the Fermi-LAT galactic center $\gamma$ -ray excess is a manifestation of the look-elsewhere effect– have we caught the Milky Way’s GC at an (in)opportune time? Furthermore, are there signatures that can distinguish this scenario from other explanations of the galactic center excess?

This letter is structured as follows. We first provide a brief description of the simulations and the methods used to model $\gamma$ -ray emission from the simulated CRs, and define the baseline “templates” used to calculate residuals at given snapshots of the simulations. We then present the range of residual spectra and morphologies that occur due to time-dependent CR transport. Finally, we show how transient behavior in the GC diffuse $\gamma$ -ray emission can mimic the measured Fermi-LAT galactic center excess, and discuss the implications of this result.

## II Methods

We analyze a set of three simulations of Milky Way (MW)-like galaxies (labeled m12f, m12i, and m12m), first introduced in [17], run with FIRE-2 physics and multi-species, spectrally-resolved cosmic rays. These galaxies are simulated from cosmological initial conditions at $z\sim 100$ , and evolved to late times with the single-bin fluid CR treatment described in [8, 18]; at redshift $z=0.05$ , the simulations are reinitialized with CR spectra for protons, electrons, anti-protons, positrons, and heavier nuclei using spectral shapes and relative normalizations from local ISM observations. CR are produced by supernovae, with 10% of pre-ejecta kinetic energy going into the CRs, and 2% of that energy into the leptons. These simulated galaxies have been widely studied by members of the FIRE collaboration, and have been demonstrated to be good MW analogs in a variety of metrics. However, we ultimately do not consider m12i in this work due to this specific realization featuring a significant warp in the disk that is not compatible with the MW’s morphology (see [32]). The two remaining galaxies, m12f and m12m, are both Milky Way-mass spiral galaxies; m12f has a flatter, extended disk, and m12m has a more pronounced galactic bulge.

We model diffuse $\gamma$ -ray emission from $\Pi^{0}$ decay, non-thermal relativistic Bremsstrahlung, and inverse Compton scattering in the simulations according to the procedure described in [32]. We note that both m12f and m12m have higher star formation rates (SFRs) within the central $\sim$ kpc than that observed in the MW, resulting in a factor of a few to 10 times more diffuse $\gamma$ -ray flux than that observed by Fermi-LAT (Figure 1). However, the star formation rates in both galaxies are highly variable over time; past analysis of simulations with the same initial conditions but different FIRE physics showed that the SFR of m12f is consistent with that of the Milky Way’s Central Molecular Zone at some snapshots [29]. It is likely that including active galactic nuclei (AGN) feedback would suppress the SFR in the GC, but for the purpose of isolating effects due to different sources of CRs, we do not include AGN in these simulations. We do not model $\gamma$ -ray emission from either DM annihilation or decay, or from a millisecond pulsar population; the focus of this work is the time-variability of diffuse $\gamma$ -ray from known stellar sources.

*Figure 1: The $\gamma$ -ray spectrum in the central $10^{\circ}$ region of interest (ROI) for simulated galaxies m12f and m12m; the median value of the spectrum across 460-20 Myr in lookback time is shown in the solid and dashed lines, respectively. The shaded regions indicate the full range of spectra over the same time span. The measured Fermi-LAT $\gamma$ -ray spectrum in the same ROI of the Milky Way is shown by the black dotted line. While features of the $\gamma$ -ray spectra for the simulated galaxies show similarities to the measured spectrum, such as a peak below 1 GeV and a similar slope of the high-energy tail, the simulated spectra are an order-of-magnitude larger, due to the greater number of stellar sources of CRs in the simulations compared to the Milky Way. These features are discussed in detail in [32].*

The principal exercise of this work is to compare the $\gamma$ -ray emission at each simulation snapshot to a baseline “template” that approximates steady-state $\gamma$ -ray emission in the galactic center. We construct the baseline template as follows: we calculate the total $\gamma$ -ray flux in the region of interest (ROI) for each simulation snapshot. A snapshot is defined as having “low-burstiness” if the total flux at that snapshot is below the median value across all snapshots for that simulation. The baseline template is the mean of the low-burstiness snapshots (Figure 2). The “residuals” considered are the difference between the flux at a given snapshot and the baseline template.

*Figure 2: The baseline diffuse $\gamma$ -ray emission template for galaxy m12f (top), and galaxy m12m (bottom) shown in three different energy channels (0.1 GeV, 3 GeV, and 10 GeV). The template is constructed by taking the mean value of flux for snapshots in which the total $\gamma$ -ray flux in the ROI is less than the median across all snapshots for that simulation. Note that the template for m12f is slightly brighter than the template for m12m, although both templates have comparable morphologies and disk thicknesses.*

At each snapshot, we compare the diffuse $\gamma$ -ray spectrum and morphology in the ROI to that of the baseline template, considering both 10∘ and 20∘ ROIs. The center of the galaxy is defined as the mass-weighted centroid of star particles in the simulation. Additionally, to determine the effect of diffuse emission along the line-of-sight, we consider three different radial cuts on the data ( $r_{\rm{cut}}$ = 0, 2, and 7 kpc), with $r_{\rm{cut}}$ defined as distance from the observer.

## III Results

### III.1 Overview

In this section, we consider both the spectral shape and morphology of the residual $\gamma$ -ray flux relative to the baseline template. For both galaxies m12f and m12m, the spectrum and morphology of the residuals is highly variable over time, for all configurations of ROI and radial cuts considered. Excesses relative to the baseline template are commonly much larger in magnitude than the measured Fermi-LAT excess (Figure 3). In general, the 10∘ ROI shows more variability over time than the larger 20∘ ROI; this is due to the inclusion of regions of the galactic disk and the Fermi bubble-like structures that begin to appear between 10-20∘ in latitude and can persist for 10s of Myrs (see [33] for discussion of these features). In general, more stringent cuts to emission along the line-of-sight result in more variation in the residuals. We compare to the Fermi-LAT galactic center excess within a 10∘ ROI shown in [1]; we include the high-energy tail of this excess in order to consider the possibility that it may reflect time-dependent phenomena from CRs.

Galaxy m12f displays more variation in the residual spectra at high energies relative to galaxy m12m, which is more variable at lower ( $<$ 10 GeV) energies. These behaviors reflect differences in the morphology of the two galaxies: m12m has a more distinct galactic bar and bulge, as well as a burstier star formation history, which result in greater variation in the gas density (and thus $\Pi^{0}$ decay) over time. m12f has a more uniform star formation history, and changes to the high-energy tail of the $\gamma$ -ray spectrum are driven primarily by changing radiation and magnetic field strength over time, which preferentially affect losses due to synchrotron and inverse Compton scattering [32].

The morphology of the residual $\gamma$ -ray flux across all snapshots most commonly results in similar excesses and deficits across the 0.1 GeV, 3 GeV, and 10 GeV energy channels (Figure 4, top). There are also snapshots that feature an excess in one or two channels that is not present in the third (Figure 4, bottom). The excesses can vary from 1 degree to greater than 10 degrees in diameter, and can occur anywhere within the galactic disk (i.e. wherever a supernova or cluster of supernovae has recently occurred). In the following subsections, we consider several examples that illustrate classes of behaviors.

*Figure 3: The range of spectra of residuals for galaxies m12f (top) and m12m (bottom), in $10^{\circ}$ (left) and $20^{\circ}$ (right) ROIs; the shaded region shows the 25th and 75th percentiles from snapshots across a 460 to 20 Myr span. Different radial cuts ( $r_{\rm{cut}}=$ 0, 2, and 7 kpc) are shown by the different colored regions (blue, pink, and green, respectively). The measured Fermi-LAT excess in the $10^{\circ}$ ROI is shown by the black dotted line. For all combinations of ROIs and radial cuts considered, the measured Fermi-LAT excess falls comfortably within the 25th and 75th percentiles, with many residuals considerably larger in magnitude.*

### III.2 Example 1: Large starburst

*Figure 4: Top: An example of residual flux for m12m in which a large, central starburst creates similar excesses in the 0.1, 3, and 10 GeV channels. Bottom: An example of residual flux for m12m at an earlier snapshot in time, in which a pair of smaller starbursts produce an excess in the 3 and 10 GeV channels that is absent in the 0.1 GeV channel. In both cases, the excesses are surrounded by deficits in flux relative to the template, due to the supernovae vacating the gas in their surrounding regions.*

We first consider a snapshot in galaxy m12m, in which there is a significant uptick in star formation within the central kpc in the last 50 Myr of the simulation, leading to a large starburst and an increase in $\gamma$ -ray flux. The residual flux in this snapshot is centered, and extends for approximately 8 degrees in latitude and 12 degrees in longitude. The residuals are nearly identical in shape and magnitude across the 0.1 GeV, 3 GeV, and 10 GeV channels.

Notably, a deficit in $\gamma$ -ray flux relative to the template occurs within the plane of the galactic disk, on either side of the central excess. This feature results from the starburst pushing gas away from the galactic center, vacating the surrounding region. These deficits are a common feature across the range of residual maps produced in this analysis, and nearly always appear next to or surrounding an excess in flux.

### III.3 Example 2: Excess present in higher energy channels and absent from low energy channel

In this snapshot, which occurs earlier in the evolution of galaxy m12m, there is an excess in flux present in the 3 GeV and 10 GeV channels, which does not appear in the 0.1 GeV channel. This residual pattern is the result of two events that occurred within proximity of each other in space and time, one centered at 0∘ in longitude, and the other at 5∘. This configuration creates an environment in which CR loss rates are more rapid for $\Pi^{0}$ decay and relativistic Bremsstrahlung (which both depend on gas density) than for ICS, which contributes approximately equally in all three channels [32].

### III.4 Example 3: Centered excess with similarities to GCE

*Figure 5: Residual spectra for galaxy m12f for a subset of samples over an 100 Myr timespan. The measured Fermi-LAT $\gamma$ -ray excess is shown by the black dotted line. One spectrum similar to the Fermi-LAT excess is indicated by a thicker line; this is the example explored in Section III.4, and depicted in Figure 6. This set of residuals show a wide variety of shapes and amplitudes, indicating that “excesses” can occur at any range of energies between 0.1 and 100 GeV.*

This snapshot of galaxy m12f corresponds to a residual spectrum that is comparable in amplitude and shape to the measured Fermi-LAT excess (Figure 5). The morphology of the residual flux is approximately spherical within the central 10∘ in the 3 GeV and 10 GeV channels, with some of the excess extending out to 20∘ (Figure 6). However, within the 20∘ ROI, deficits occur beside the excesses within the plane of the galactic disk, as observed in the two prior examples. This snapshot displays the most dynamical environment and complexity of the illustrative examples considered in this paper: the $\gamma$ -ray flux is the product of at least three clusters of supernovae occurring separately within the disk. This configuration is comparable to the multiple leptonic outburst scenario explored in [9]; however, here, the outbursts are still predominantly hadronic, with differences in CR loss times driven by the properties of the multi-phase ISM, with spatial and temporal inhomogeneities in gas density, magnetic and radiation field strength, cosmic ray flux, and star formation rates. While galaxy m12f is not a perfect Milky Way analog, we present this snapshot as an example of a scenario in which a complex, highly dynamical astrophysical environment can produce a residual flux that is phenomenologically similar to the observed Fermi-LAT galactic center $\gamma$ -ray excess, simply from non-equilibrium CR transport.

## IV Discussion and Implications for the observed galactic center $\gamma$ -ray excess

The purpose of this exercise is to determine the extent to which time-dependent cosmic-ray transport can affect the interpretation of diffuse $\gamma$ -ray emission within the galactic center. Indeed, by comparing the diffuse emission at each snapshot to a baseline template approximating steady-state equilibrium, we find transient bumps and wiggles in the residual $\gamma$ -ray spectra occurring at all energies between 0.1 and 100 GeV. We show these residuals for a subset of 10 snapshots for galaxy m12f in Figure 5; the full range of residuals are even more variable in shape and amplitude. Within just this 100 Myr span, there are both deficits and excesses, some significantly larger than the measured Fermi-LAT excess, without a global, monotonic trend.

These residual excesses are driven by both star formation and its effects on the surrounding environment within the galactic center, and time-dependent CR transport. Within the central kpc, the CR diffusion time is approximately $\tau_{\rm{diff}}\sim(1\rm{\,kpc})^{2}/3\times 10^{29}\rm{cm^{2}\,s^{-1}}\sim$ 1 Myr, which is comparable to the time scale on which the ISM and the GC $\gamma$ -ray spectrum change. Thus, there is typically not sufficient time for CRs injected by supernovae to diffuse throughout the galactic center and reach a globally uniform distribution before the intervening medium is disrupted. Moreover, the efficiencies of the relevant CR loss mechanisms scale differently with CR energy, and have different dependencies on the properties of the local ISM; for instance, inverse Compton and synchrotron loss times are shorter than the $\Pi^{0}$ decay loss time at 10 GeV [17, 32]. The differing energy and density dependencies of these loss channels mean that local inhomogeneities in the ISM produce spatially and spectrally variable $\gamma$ -ray emission that cannot be captured by smooth, averaged templates.

Moreover, the two simulations considered in this work use our favored model for CR transport as found in [17] (i.e., the CR injection spectrum and scattering rate are both power-law functions of momentum/rigidity, with $j(R)\propto R^{-4.2}$ and $\bar{\nu}\propto\bar{\nu}_{0}R^{-0.5}$ , where $\bar{\nu}_{0}\approx 10^{-9}\ \rm{s}^{-1}$ ). While this model has been shown to reproduce constraints on CR transport from local ISM observations, including proton and electron spectra, the boron-to-carbon ratio, and the electron-to-proton ratio, it is far from the only viable model of CR transport [19]. Indeed, other analytical and numerical studies have considered a wide range of physically-motivated models of CR transport that depend on plasma properties [38, 37, 2, 3, 6]. These models, which may have non-uniform CR injection spectra or dependence on magnetic field substructure, are likely to produce more small-scale variation than is present in our simulations; thus, our work likely underestimates variation in the galactic center due to small-scale inhomogeneities in the plasma.

Despite these limitations, the results of this exercise have important implications for the interpretation of the Fermi GCE. The most conservative interpretation of this exercise is that, by using analysis tools that implicitly assume steady-state equilibrium for cosmic ray propagation, past analyses of the Fermi-LAT observations of the Milky Way’s galactic center have significantly underestimated astrophysical uncertainties arising from completely mundane sources. A more radical interpretation of this exercise is that an uptick in diffuse emission can explain the observed galactic center $\gamma$ -ray excess without invoking either annihilating or decaying dark matter, or a novel population of pulsars. In this scenario, the Fermi-LAT galactic center $\gamma$ -ray excess would be the result of the “look-elsewhere effect”. The Milky Way’s galactic center is the only such region of any galaxy that the Fermi-LAT can observe in detail, and it could be merely a coincidence that, at present, the observed spectrum contains a 1-10 GeV excess. In either case, it is imperative to re-evaluate the templates used in analyses of Fermi-LAT data, and, if necessary, devise new templates and methods that can fully capture the effects of time-dependent CR transport as well as a wider range of astrophysical configurations. Both GALPROP and empirical template-fitting approaches (the latter of which are often calibrated to GALPROP) share similar limitations in this regard; both assume smooth distributions of stars, gas, magnetic field structure, and radiation fields, and, as static solvers, exclude time dependence by construction [7, 11, 1]. Thus, neither of these standard approaches is capable of capturing the time-dynamical effects discussed in this work.

A limitation of this exercise is that it is based on a sample of two simulations that, while analogous to the Milky Way in many aspects, are not identical to it. As discussed in Section II, of particular concern is the star formation rate in the central kpc of these simulations, which is, throughout the period of the simulation considered, 1-2 orders of magnitude higher than the star formation rate in the Milky Way’s Central Molecular Zone (CMZ). The higher star formation rate correlates to a higher supernova rate, and thus the ROI within these simulations may be more violent than the same region within the Milky Way. Previous studies have demonstrated that including a central black hole similar to Sagittarius A* and various channels of AGN feedback, including CR-dominated jets, can suppress star formation in L* galaxies [28, 39, 35, 36]. While including a central AGN in these simulations would likely lower the star formation rate, the injection of CRs by AGN jets would likely also contribute to small-scale and temporal variability in diffuse $\gamma$ -ray emission. Moreover, with only two simulated galaxies, we cannot robustly quantify the frequency with which mundane CR physics produces residuals resembling the Fermi GCE, which would be necessary to make a rigorous statistical statement about the look-elsewhere effect. Ultimately, we intend for this work to serve as a relatively simple proof-of-concept that can be replicated on other galaxy simulations with varying CR and AGN physics, as well as different star formation histories and galactic center geometries, in order to determine how sensitive these time-dependent effects are to particular choices of CR transport models.

If other galactic centers are found to have excesses at other ranges in the $\gamma$ -ray spectrum (including in the MeV and TeV ranges), this evidence would strongly bolster a time-dependent astrophysical explanation; if other galactic centers all contained a 1-10 GeV excess, then such observations would make a compelling argument in favor of the dark matter explanation. While such data does not exist at present, future observations from the Cherenkov Telescope Array Observatory (CTAO), the Compton Spectrometer and Imager (COSI), or a next-generation space-based $\gamma$ -ray telescope may be able to shed light on these various hypotheses. In light of the results of this study, we argue that time-dependent CR transport should be seriously considered as a source of at least part of the observed Fermi-LAT galactic center $\gamma$ -ray excess. A future exercise that would be highly informative in testing this scenario would be to apply the templates and CR-propagation models used to analyze the Fermi GCE to these simulations. Because we know the truth values of CR and $\gamma$ -ray flux, gas column density, magnetic fields, as well as the dark matter density and astrophysical J-factor in the simulation, we would be able to compare the best-fit model and identify specific failure modes.
